NEW YEAR IN THE COLONIES. Across the great dividing seas We stretch a kindly hand, To where Canadian rivers freeze In the wild IN estern land: O'er Afric's deathly deserts wide, To shores of far Japan, Where scarce a living soul dares bide, Except an Englishman: Hid in Australian sheep-farms lone, And South Sea Islands strange, Or under India's torrid zone, We find them, without change: The same warm, honest British heart, The same strong British hand, And New year's blessings, though apart, Ring round from land to land. Autlun- of John Halifax, Gentleman.

DEAWN BI T' RIBBLE SIDE. (Air: "Love at gorne.") - When the settin' sun shines breet O'er the silver tide, Oft aw stray wr lingerin' feet ; Deawn bi t' Ribble side. , While the wavelets whisper near,: • Aw con shed a lonely tear O'er rni youthful days so dear,. Deawn bi t' Ribble side. Silvery tide, sweetly glide; Bring me back those youthful days, Deawa bi t' Ribble side!

Here aw use' to laugh an' play, Full o' boyish pride:— Like a dreeom id seems to-day, Deawn bi t' Ribble side. Playmates' voices dear an' strong, Dear youfig faces cherished long, Use' to mek a merry throng 12/sawn bi t' Ribble side, Silvery tide. sweetly glide; Bring me back those merry days, Deawn bit' Ribble side'. There one neet the stars did shine O'er ml promised bride, When hoo gave her heart for mine, Deown bi t' Ribble side. Two true hearts 'at love med one, Grew moor fond as time rolled on, While sweet ehilder's faces shone, Deawn bi t' Ribble side. Silvery tide, sweetly glide; Bring me back those lovelit days. Deawn bi t' Ribble side!

Some are gone to foreign :ands, O'er the ocean wide— Only one owd skoomate stands Deawn bi t' Ribble side. Owd an' lonely, soon aw'll creep Wheer yo' see you grey Church peep, Theer ml wife an' childer sleep, Deawn bi t' Ribble Silvery tide, sweetly glide; Sing for ever o'er ml grave, Deawn bi t' Ribble side! Higher Walton. Jan. 4th„ 1888. GEORGIE HULL.

Hard thing to sharpen—The water's edge. A railv ay strike—Tapping the carriage wheels. Of interest to mothers—A switch in time saves nine. On what supposition could a pocket-handkerchief build a house ?--If it became brick (cambric). The minister fulished his discourse, and sat down, and the choir rose and sang, "It is time to awake from sleep." Shakspere revised :—" All the world's a stage, and most of the men and women in the business are merely
supers." Home, in a measure. is what the presiding spirit of the family makes it—the brightest or the gloomiest spot

on earth. - If you were willing to be as pleasant and as anxious to please in your own home as you are in the company of your neighbours, you wonld have the happiest home in the world. Don't judge a man's character by the deference shown him. No one ever saw a chimney-sweep crowded off the Torment. Most people," says Sydney Smith, " aro willing to play the Good Samaritan, but without the oil and the twopence." First Friend: "Did von get her photograph while you were away ?" Second Friend: " Well—ali—the fact is she gave me her negative." A neat proposal of marriage was made by a young man the other night, who seid, "Now, Miss Smythe, you say you have £l,OOO in your own name; why not put it in mine ? " It is the best, because the most bonpvoloot, good breed- ing which, without regard to personal preference, deals to all in general society an equal, or at least a fair, measure of social attention. Every man lives for others as well as himself; and while the tenor of his lite should be that of cheerful in- dustry In his calling, he should keep open every avenue to compassion and liberality. The business of such a man is habitual, and includes no unreasonable cares; his benevolence is uniform, and finds opportunities for exercise. He lives reputably, and is beloved by his +contemporaries. In this way he secures a fair share of

happiness. THE BEGINNINGS OF JAPANESII ART.—The critic and historiarn who is yet to write the story of art in Japan, from prehistoric time to this twentieth year of Meiji (civilization in enlightened peace), will discriminate nicely between what is borrowed and what is original. The folding fan, modelled on the beta wing, the arts of lacquering, sword-making, cloisonne on .porcelain, and some of the methods of decorating faience are of native origin; but of bronze casting and the secrets of alloy, nielle, and metallic work, tell-tale philology often betrays i a Corean, Chinese, Persian, or Indian origin. Bronze s "Chinese metal," and some of the names of tools and , processes, as I learned them in the shops, are but mis- pronounced Corean. Beni, or Benigari (rouge), seems to point to Bengal, just as briki, for "blink," is only the Dutch word for tin in the mouth of the man who eschews the letter 1. The shapes and models of old temple orna- ments and flower vases point unmistakably to Persian origin, even as the native annals report Japanese em- bassies meeting those from Persia at the court of the Middle Kingdom. lira ziers, incense-holders, water-tanks, standing lanterns, memorial tablets, and tomb-doors give abundance of opportunity to the bronzist to show his skill in handling masses of metal. The images of Great Buddha at Nara, Kamakura, and elsewhere, show what Cellinis of Japan can achieve in colossal works of art.—Screirner's Magazine for January. Sus KNEW His.—He was one of the very trimmest, and daintiest young men imaginable, and he was in his element as escort to six ultra-fashionable young ladies on a little picnic excursion. There was an antiquated hut keen-eyed woman from the rural districts also on board the train. "I say, girls," said the brilliant young man, "see me make a mash of the old lady in the sun- bonnet," and he skipped across the aisle, tipped his hat and said, blandly, while all the girls giggled—" Ah, good day, madam; beg pardon, but haven't I seen you be- fore?" She gave him one look, and grabbed both his soft little hands in her own brown toil-worn hands. "Of course you have," she said, gleefully, pulling him into the seat beside her. "You're Mr. Hildybrand Day Grolyer, hey ?" Alas ! he was Mr. Hildehrand de Golyer. "I knowed you the minit I set eves on you. You're the very young man that boarded with me a month in tile country last summer a year ago, and von went off and forgot to pay your board, didn't you I've been look- ing for you ever since, and I'm mighty glad to see you. The bill is just thirty-six dollars and ninety-five cents, countin' in your washin' and mendin' that I done my- self; and I want von to hand it right over 'fore you git off'n this seat. We'll call it thirty-six even for cash." And he hadn't but seven dollars and forty-one cents to his name. There are some scenes in real life too painful to even write about. This is one of them. We draw the veil on it right here. Poor Hildebrand I—American. ORIGIN OF "Tax STRANGE CASH OF DR. JEKYLL AND HYDE."—I can but give an instance or so of what part is done sleeping and what part awake, and leave the reader to share what laurels there are, at his own nod, between myself and my collaborators; and to do this I will first take a book that a number of persons have been polite enough to read, the Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. I had long been trying to write a story on this subject, to find a body, a vehicle, for that strong sense of man's double being which must at times come in upon and Overwhelm the mind of every , thinking creature. I had even written one, The Travel- ling Companion, which was returned by an editor on the plea that it was a work of genius and indecent, and which I burned the other day on the ground that it FIRS not a work of genius, and that Jeku// had supplanted it. Then came one of those financial fluctuations to which (with an elegant modesty) I have hitherto referred in the third person. For two days I went about racking my brains for a plot of any sort; and on the second night I dreamed the scene at the window, and a scene afterward split in two, in which Hyde, pur- sued for some crime, took the powder and underwent the change in the presence of his pursuers. All the rest was made awake, and ccinsciously, although I think I can trace in much of it the manner of my Brownies. The meaning of the tale is therefore mine, and had long Pre-existed In my garden of Adonis, and tried one body after another in vain; indeed, I do most of the morality, worse luck! and my Brownies have not a rudiment of what we call a conscience. Mine, too, is the setting, mine the characters. All that was given me was the matter of three scones, and the central idea of a voluntary change becoming involuntary. Will it be thought un- generous, after I have been so liberally ladling out praise to my unseen collaborators, if I here toss them over, bound hand and foot, into the arena of the critics? For the business of the powders, which so many have cen- sured, is, I am relieved to say, not mine at all but the Brownies' .—Robert Louis Stevenson, in Scribner's Magazine. STRAITS. • A MIGUATION OF. THE WOODCOCK. 'iv JOHN PEERS. Next morning Tuesday—came the 'question : What next? To sea or not to sea? that is the ques- tion, whether it be wiser in this boat to suffer the gibes and jeers of riparian gods. or. boldly dare Old Neptune to oppose? And we decided in the nega- tive, in order to give the weather another chance to declare - itself; for though the morning -was bright and fine, and altogether pleasant, the sky, last evening, after the bit of a breeze, was full of "mare's tails "—eirroll4 of large size, signs of wind past, present, or to come. . But which in this case? there's the rub!!' It was decided by the unanimous voice of a council of one that the River Dee required exploring, and that we werethe pc-pie to do it. So we left the littleharbour and the berth where, last evening, so many eager eyes looked down upon us and our domestic arrangements and commenting freely but politely thereon in the ancient language of Britain. So, into the broad river we turned, now filled by a nice little tide. Before a very light northernly breeze, we slowly stemmed the young ebb, then mak- ing up "Greenfield gutter until we found the relative proportions of sand and water, as required fbr the purposes of navigation, inverted. Where we wanted plenty of water and little sand, we got little water and plenty of sand and that increasing. So, having no superstitious reverence for the waters of St Winefred, and not wishing to try its efficacy on our maladies, which probably belong more to the province of the psychologist than the physician, we returned. Besides. the saint as perhaps becomes a lady, is rather exacting in the matter of trophies. One has seen beneath the roof of the little cupola that covers the welling waters of the Holy Spring. derelict appliancies of invalid locomotion. The sticks, crutches and bearing barrows which had brought thelame and halt to these Ii sating waters were left behind is witnesses to the miracle and trophies to the Saint Now if we had been weak enough to try the effects ot these miracle-working waters and thereby become possessed of sound minds in sound bodies, we should in honour be coin- polled to leave the poor old Woodcock as an offeringl to the Saint, whilst we waded asbere. There were objections to this course, so we rininded •the boat and began to go with the,stream (of 21 tons per minute) which the Well• of St. Winefred supplies, A. "flat," which had been slowly following us. still pursued her devious way, whilst we sought deeper. and less sandy waters. We ran down the river and then headed over towards Dawpool on the Cheshire side. • About half-way across we CAM up with a wreck— submerged—except the mast. A desolate and deserted wreck, unnoticed and unvisited—save perhaps by the solitary sea-bird, who will take nothing but may leavethat which will mark his presence on fhe spot, or the equally solitary fisherman, who may take a few inches of cord as a souvenir. All this shows that this is no place for any vessel having duo regard for her reputation and posthumous honours, to subside in. For, had this poor mis-guided bark but chosen the other side of the peninsula, in the waters of the Mersey (which are not strained), she would have had the honour of being at- tended, night and day, by one if not two vessels and their crews. She would receive official recognition, and might also be the recipient of polite attention from a burly individual in flannels, who, in order the better to make her aquaintance, would proceed to invest his am- ple form in a suit of rubber, a pair of lead soled clogs and a copper helmet. Evidently this is no place for us to submerge! We'll go further though we fare worse. So we ran over to Dawpool and landed there, geologised —bouldered—and drifted. We ran up the cliff and down the cliff, and then had a photo shot at the cliff, and it in revenge, came out over exposed! We remained at anchor off Dawpool until the evening, poking about among the boulders, shells, and living things of the beach ; indeed I think we decended so low, literally and ethically as to collect periwinkles ! ! but I will not burden my conscience by asserting that we ate them with a pin—no, from that enormity at least we refrained. For I think it is adding insult to injury first to put the poor things to a cruel death by boiling., and then having extracted the shrunken remains by a pin, to hold the torturous victim up to meet the jeers of an unfeeling world! The moral aspects of this question of Molluscocide are well worth the attention of moral philosophers, and also of those humane persons who, merely as an act of charity, make their own bodies the sepulchre of these twisted sea-snails. But we must leave this vext question, for the tide is at the flood, the day is on the wane, and red-sailed f.sh- ing boats are fleeting home impelled by a fair wind and a favouring tide. Parkgate was their destination ; and already the narrow deep is pleasantly dotted by their red sails now brightened by the rays of the reclining sun. We also, must seek a resting place for the night; so the anchor was weighed, the sails trimmed, and we joined the homeward bound procession. Up the rapidly shoaling and narrowing deep we followed the lead of our guides until we came to where the water was only sufficiently deep to float us. Here by advice we stopped, nor dared the dangers of the shoaly "deep" to reach the wave worn walls of this old-time entrepot of the Irish passenger traffic, the Holyhead of our great grettistgrand- fathers. The tide quickly attained its maximlim ; as quickly receded and left us aground for the night. Ap- parently my two shipmates, Alf. and the P. regarded this as a providential dispensation, enabling them to visit the remains of ancient grandeur as displayed by this decayed watering place. To anticipatea little—they returned charged to the muzzle with glowing accounts of the antique glories of this once fashionable sea side resort; how memories of Royalties and notables (Han- del amongst them) of fashionables and their attendant follies, still linger about the place. The accounts they ' discharged upon me as the only and .unresisting victim. Meanwhile I engaged myself in barefooted and bare- legged pattering about the boat. The little water still trickling past her and the favouring list she had assumed suggested and encouraged a scrub. This was soon ao- complished on the upturned side, and I was leaning against the boat, scrub in hand, drinking in the beauties of the evening, when I became aware of the presence of a burly stranger. "Sir," said he, "the contemplation of nature does not appear to be conducive to the continuance of your labour. "The task I set myself, doctor," said I, for it was indeed the author of " Rassellas," he of the diction- ary, "is finished, but if you think you can mend it here is The scrub." "I believe," said the didactic one, "in the dignity of labour,.but have no present aptitude for the employ- ment. But, sir," continued he, "if I presume not ' on so short an acquaintance, what ma:,, be the induce- ment to choose the damp habitation•of a boat in ex- change for the more civilised comforts of a home?" ' Briefly I recounted to this lover of Fleet-street our aim: and object—health and recreation; that my two ship- mates had gone ashore in search of the latter; inciden- tally I happened to mention my fear that the P. did not enjoy with that fulness of satisfaction I could have wished, the many and frequent opportunities I had af- forded him of mud-larking and sand-honping ; that having the occidental fever in his blood, and the distant and still to be sought beauties of Orme. the Puffin, and the Straits ever before his eyes. induced in him a frame of mind unfitted for the full appreciation of present blessings. Now in this I soon sound I had, un- consciously been playing the part of Boswell. and had furnished the great Cham of literature "with a theme upon which to expatiate. And straightway he pro- ceeded to make my friend the P. a peg upon which to hang a discourse upon the evil of allowing the imagina- tion to sway the judgment. As is usual in such cases, the good doctor id sonic violence to his text when he made my friend the P., whom I have always found to be characterised by "a sweet reasonableness,'' the subject of such a homily. "Sir," said the doctor, "your friend's is a slight mental disorder that prevents his enjoying and

ThepoOr and afflicted ought not to be made the victims of experiments in spiritual quackery, especially as the services of the mortal and much maligned physician are thought to '.'be good enough ia cases of sickness in thecharlatan's ownfamily. My belief ins quack :would be ranch hastened by seeing him swallowing his own nostrums." "Aye, ave," I broke in, "but if that prescription were rigidly enforced, the species would soon be extmct—and the tolls in our market die-Placed ".•—• t Whether the antiaipatedcatastrophe thus foreshadowed startled me into a juster appreciation if the realities of my Surroundings I will not say, but when .I looked round my visitor was gone, and the next sound I heard was the view halo! of my returning mates. Then they emptied the vials of their investigations upon my devoted head, "and into the porches of mine ears did pour," and stunned me by the report before men- tioned. Thanks to a good tough constitution, and a free passage from ear to ear, I survived the dire infliction. We uprighted the boat, and packed the bilges with sand to keep an even beam, and to render her more comfort- able for habitation and repose. And thus a lovely evening brought to a fitting close a lovely day. . Early next morning we left this shallow place for the deeper waters of Dawpool, where we experienced a slight shower, memorable as the last for many days; and through Welshman's Gut to the Mostyn side, where the stronger ebb gave the effect of an increased bree' ze and to us steerage Way and an increased speed. Past the red-hulled river Dec lightship—where we left our last newspaper—old to us, bet fresh and welcome to that iso- lated crew ; past the little dumpy Bell Buoy, now slqwly tolling its unheeded warning; over the rollicking white horses, then so playfully gambolling upon Chester Bar; out into the open sea, where' the river tide hitherto favouring us being spent, we found the wind fall light, and our progress very slow. Slowly receded the red- banded Point of Air Lighthouse, and the tall shaft of Prestytvn. Slowly appeared and slowly receded . the Pier of ithyl, and still far in the West the blue head of Orme appeared to be as far as ever from attainnient. Gradually the light northerly wind and the gentle,. but shoreward pulsating heave of the. water, set us in shore; and after eight hours' sailing we found ourselves com- pelled to anchor in the beautiful but exposed Bey of Colwyn. The P. took advantage of our stay here to go ashore and do business in the metals—he wired home and bought some tinned fruit. When the flood-tide no longer op- posed, we took to the oars—the wind being now con- spicuous by its absence and the sea likeglass—and rowed round the Little Orme's Head into the cliff-bound Bay of Llandudno.

WARRINGTON STARR - BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY. The first annual meeting of the members of the first, Warrington (826th) Starr-Bowkett Building Society was held on Wednesday evening in Legh-st. schoolroom. Mr. R. A. Naylor presided. There was a large attendance, the directors present being Messrs. N. Legge, H. Sutton, T. Burton, GI Lea, W. Crampton, J. Griffiths, and D. Sumner. In the course of a short address 'rho CnenimAti said he did not know that he had dived ' vary minutely into the details of that wonderful build- ing society, but he had heard from people well able to form an opinion in other towns that these societies were really formed on a satisfactory financial basis, and from what he could see of the balance sheet, which was the first the board of management had presented to them, that particular society appeared to be in a very flourish- ing condition, and had a bright future before it. (Ap- plause.) It appeared from the report that during the year 341 members had been enrolled, holding 737 shares, and he understood that since the report was printed the number of members had increased to 374, holding 818 shares. (Hear, bear.) The directors seemed to be very well satisfied indeed with the first year's working, and he hoped and trusted that their an- ticipations for the future might be more than realised. They all knew that the last few years had been very bad ones for all kinds of building societies, whether they. I were those called permanent associations or those fauLled on that modern system. The trade of the coutttry had been in the most depressed condition, and working men had not had very much money, to spare, because their wages had been considerably diminished. But he understood from gentlemen in a position to give aa opinion they were now on the eve of better times. (Applause.) He had been speaking to a number of gen- tlemen interested in the various branches of industry in this country—men who turned over a great many thou- sands of pounds yearly—and he heard from a variety of sources that the year 1888, so far as trade was con- cerned, was likely to be better than any year they had , had since 1871. (Applause.) Referring to the advant- ages of building societies, Mr. Naylor remarked that if they could get people to have something at stake in the country they would, of course, create a greater amount of interest in the affairs of the country, and if people had something at stake there would be no fear of their turning into Socialists. He knew that the doctrines of Socialism were preached up and down this country at the present time, and one of its main doctrines, he pre- sumed, was that they should all divide amongst each other. (Laughter.) If a workingman had been so in- dustrious as to save his shillings And sixpences and got some property together, it was not very 'likely that ne would turn into a Socialist and divide with the man who had spent his money on what was not worth the money. Looking at it in that point of view, they were doing a good thing for the nation and a good thing for the town in which they lived when they encouraged a society like that Starr-Bowkett Building Society. (Ap- plause.) The chairman then read a letter from the auditors of the society, stating that during the financial year just ended the books of the society had been very satisiactorily kept, and that they Must thank the secre- tary (Mr. Titchett) for the very ready manner in which he had rendered them assistance in their work.—The SEcesraiiv then read the first annual report and balance sa(et of the board of management. They had pleasure in submitting this report, feeling confident that it would meet with the approval and ready acceptance of all members. During the . year 341 members r had been enrolled, holding 737 shares; of these seven had allowed their subscriptions to be forfeited. thus leaving the present number of paying members 334. 'The total income for the year from all sources was £824 12s 114 d. During the year appropriations had been made amounting to £9OO, £5OO of which had been taken up. The profits on the first year's working amounted to £6 17s. 24d. (Applause.)—The report and balance sheet was then adopted unanimously.—The retiring directors, Messrs. G. Lea, W. Crampton, J. Griffiths, and ). Sum- ner were next re-elected, as were also the auditors, Messrs.,W. Mullard and F. Pearson.—The fourth appro- priation In connection with the society, was then made, and it resulted in Mr. S. G. Holmes Lovely-lane, being entitled to a sum of £4OO for a period of 124 years free of interest.—The proceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

CHAPTEII XVII. FREE AT LAST. • Anne presented iter,,elf at Exeter g,nol next day, passed tliroughi. the gloomy corridors, with the grim- faced warders unlocking ma.ive door,: to let her through, arld-thert locking them again Vehind her, and entered Mattin's little;eell with a heatt fume joyful than 'is' often broo4ht to a prison., Id was a sweet and high reward for all her efforts that she should. be the, iiist messenger of peace -and good tidings' to her tirotlier, who was totally unconscious of the entire change in his fortunes.' Martin looVed!a4thimgh prison life luttlagel him at least ten -years even since Anne's lust vidit; so pale and haggard' had be grown. He greetil his sister in his usual undemonstrative fashion. "iV,ell, Anne, how are y u.lCome, sit dowmand telt Ale all the nmes. ' , But Anne/ riemained standing, still holdieg;Mar- tin's hand in IM,rs. Slie felt as though' Atte imust break eradualfy to him the tidings Ini:11 brought. e • Theatews I have to tell is very g.xxi," she-betein,- m rather a tremulous 'voice. "'Mr,Jlarriffint save we must have patience a little lenter ' • they will not set you free just 'yet, but oh, my dear Martin, nearly everything has been found out: they have artested the man they believe ,to be 'Susan's umrderer; and you will be Cleared,' • . He stood looking at his sister for a moment or two before he spoke. Then he drew a deep breath. "'Here, Anne," and he pushed a Chair towards her, "you had better sit down, and tell me the whole story." And so she told hint, and he listened almost without it word. But when elle had finished lie saiel in a low and somewhat broken voice— " And it is you who have done it all, you have done this for me. Well, you are one of those of whom it is-written, Her price is above "' but Martin, I have not quite done it all; it was Dick Lawson's mother who first found the broken sleeve-link. It is she who has been my grecttest help and comfort ever since you have been here • she said there was nothing in the world she wouldn't do for you and ine in our trouble." Anne seemed destined that day to shake her brother's composure. He had borne the news of his coming release calmly enough, but he visibly trembled now. He turned abruptly away from her, Mid then he said, without lookin,„0 round, "That woman must be a saint on earth if there ever was one. But Anne--" Martin faced her again and tried to smile, but his lips quivered, "it wouldn't be very lifted to he kind to you." • "She feels as much for you as she does for me ; she 'sail her heart was full of sorrow for you—those were her very words." ,A,geixt Martin was almost struck speechless. "If ever I come out of prison again—" was all that he could say. "You will, you will, dear I" Anne replied eagerly, "and outside your own home, there's no one will welcome you more than Mrs. Lawson.' • , The brief quarter of an hour, which was all the time allowed them by. the prison regulations, soon passed away. The moment of parting was a sorroWful- one after all.- It was hard to leave Martin still a prisoner, the date of his release uncer- tain ; possibly he would not be set free until the end of Captain Carteret's trial at the coming assizes, and, if So, Martin would have to spend his Christmas

in gaol. Anne went back to the Exeter railway station, where she had an hour-and-a-half to wait for a South-Western train to take her home. In the waiting-room were two men sitting talking together by the fire. She recognised one of them as a farmer living in the neighbourhood of St. Stephen's, but he had his back to her, and was net aware of her presence in the room. He was speaking in the loud tone of a countryman. The name of Stambridge aroused Anne's attention, and it was impossible for her not to hear what was said. "He told me and another party in confidence how it happened; he don'tmuch care te have it talked about, Stambridge don't; • it'll do him no good with the chapel folk you see; but I tell him he'll be bound to be witness at the 'sizes; and then it'll all have to come out, whether he likes it or not. You see, the afternoon before the murder happened, Stambridge , rode over to Bridestow to see a man that had a dog he'd a fancy to buy; and on his way hack, being nasty, foggy weather, he went into the Daztmoor Inn for a nrop of summat hot, and I suppose took more thau he was used to; he's a very sober man in general; but,however that may be; he got stupid like, and fairly dropped off his horse as he was corning across the moor, and there he lay for hours with his horse grazing beside of him. He got sobered after a bit, enoughto find his horse and get on him agaiu,and ride home pretty nigh starved with the cold, as you may suppose. But he's uncommon put out as to what they'll say at the chapel when they hears of it; such a man for the prayer meetings and Sunday-school as he is; and to think of him lying drunk alongside the road that very night as his poor young woman was made away with!' And here we may say farewell to James Stain- bridge. It so turned out that the fact that he was lost on the moor the night of the murder, as well as Martin Derrick, and with a less presentable reason for it, never became generally known, and Captain Stambridge's character for strict sobriety remained unaseailed. The time will speedily come, when he will find someone to console him for the loss of his Susan. "A candle is never so easily lighted again as when it has just been put out." • Anne, fearing she might be recognised, left the waiting-room, and paced up and down the platform for a while. Presently there came into fhe station, dowa Great Western train, and amidst the crowd of arrivals she saw Mr. Harrison, somewhat to her surprise, as she thought he had gone home to Tavi- stock the night before. His keen eyes speedily caught sight of Anne, and he hurried up to her, look- ing quite eager and animated. "Miss Derrick, yon are the very person I have been wanting to see a most extraordinary thing has happened. Come into the waiting-root, and I will tell you all about it, and then I am off to the prieon to see your brother. I hardly know if they will let me this evening, probably they will though, when they hear all about it, but this I can say confi- dently : Mr. Derrick will be set free to-morrow." They had got into the waiting-room by this time; it was vacant now, and they stood together by the fireplace, too excited to sit down. • I slept at Taunton la al might on my way home," began the lawyer. "I went there to see an old friend and client of mine, and it was there I heard of it. The police were bringing Captain Carteret down to Exeter last evening ; apparently by some oversight, one of the doors of the compartment they were in was left unlocked, and not very far from Taunton lie made a dash for it, and leaped on to the line. As soon as the policemen could get the train stopped they went back to look for him, and found he had fallen down an embankment in the darkness, and was lying there desperately injured—dying, in fact. They managed ta carry him to a house and got a doctor' but it was no use, and then the wretched man, finding it WR4 all over with him, said he would confess everything, and clear an innocent man; and so they fetched a magistrate and took down his depositions; and now ' I suppose by this time he is dead.". This was the story which Captain Carteret told, with' some• additional particulars which Anne learnt long afterwards. Eight years ago Francis Carteret had fallen des- perately in love with his mother's mild, Susan Derrick ; and Susan had been clever enough to make him marry her. His mother, Mrs. Norton, knew only that there was some sort of intimacy between her son and her maid, and she dismissed, Susan in disgrace. Carteret, who had, of coune,. kept his marriage secret, and who hid away Susan for a few months in London lodgings, was seen tired to death of his wife, and took the oppor- tanity of his regiment being ordered to India to get quit of her. He gave her a stun of matey down, and promised. to send her a regular allowance ; she undertaking on her side to keep the marriage still a secret until los return from India. Time went on, , ne mote nies.ey cams, and Susan could not discover her faithless liusbsinl's whereabouts. She took another situation as v's maid, and lived .comfort. ably enough with Mrs. Evelyn. When seven years had passed without heatin.,z, fro,u Francis Carteret, she learnt from the legal Invell.ook which she found in Martin's room, that s.ie emild Marry again without fear of prosecution for bigamy, although the second marriage v.•oulo not be a legal and binding one. She hesitated for some tuna, when James Stambridge offered her a home.; ilea finally made up her mind In run all risks and marry bun.

'irritation ;•• taunts -and-threats passed, 'between "'And I've been wanting tell yen ever se many them; at last be seized the revolsver which he saw above the mantel-shelf, merely to frighten her into _times., but I could never pluck up cobrage to do it before," she answered, "my heart'sr been full of • submission, so he said in his confession. At all events sorrow for yon allthese twoyears ; I could understand there was a desperate struggle between them, Susan, what you've been feeling. But now the the worst is in her mortal terror, vainly shrieking for Martin to ast, the winter is over and °one, as the Bible says. come and protect her—in another moment, Carteret ;lease God, there's brighter days coming for you and had-shot her dead. • , your dear sister." • Afterwards, in borrisr and remorse, and the wild "And for you also; Mrs. Lawson, I hope," said hope that she might still be living, he raised her nfp, M trtin. "'there shall be, if I can mike them carried her into the parlour, laid her on the so a, la Ala hters* • and tried to force brandy down her throat, from the flask which he carried in his pocket., 'The next minute lie heard carriage wheels • driving up' to the house, and then his only thought was his own safety. He extinau!sted the lamp, but he had not time to escape before Anne had entered the house, and had actually touched him, However, he get clear away without being seen by any one, thinks to the extreme , darkness oi that foggy night. In his terror of being recognised at any rail- way station, he walked the whole way back to Ply- mouth, and it was not until he carne into the lighted streetithat he discovered that—probably in the struggle with Susan--ono of his diamond sleeve links, Miss Hartley's present to.hini which he wore much against his will, bad been broken and lost, and was, perhaps, lying somewhere on. the floor of Row Tor farmhouse. Then the miserable man's punish- ment began, in Ste ever-haunting fear of detection— to end- only in a violent death. Anne took Mr. Harrison's advice, and went home by the next train. It was unlikely, he said, that the prison officials would allow her to see her brother again that day ; he, the lawyer, would remain in Exeter, and in all probability he would be able to. bring Martin, a free man, down to St. Stephen's the following afternoon. So Anne went home to bring the joyful news to Martin's faithful old servants, and then after a hasty meal she sallied forth again, weary and exhausted as she was, yet forgetting everything else in her great happiness, and she walked a raile or more, Richards accoMpanying her with a lantern through tIM dark and miry lane, to the house of Mrs. Lawson. She had the first .right to know what her discovery of the "missing link" had done for Martin. Another night and morning passed, and then Anne was once more 'at St.' Stephen's railway station, summoned by a telegram from Mr. Harrison. The train from Exeter presently drew up to the platform, a carriage door opened, and Martin sprang out. The lawyer had travelled down with him, and theeld man put his head out of the carriage window, and actually waved his hat to the brother and sister 'as he was carried onward to Taviatock. Martin held out his hand to Anne without a word, and they hurried quickly out of the little station where the stationmaster and the porters were stand- ing on the platform gaziag at the released prisoner with great interest. The trap was standing in the road outside • just as Martin had put in his port- manteau, litt'd comfortably settled Anne in her seat, . had taken the reins in his hand, and was about to drive away, there came riding by four farmers of the neighbourhood, on their return homeward after a run with the Lamerton hounds. - One and all drew bridle as they saw Martin. The news of his release had—thanks to Mrs. Lawson and to old Richards—spread far and wide already; and everybody in the place knew by this time that the real • criminal hail been -arrested, and had made full confession. Popular opinion at once swung round .with that violence which is habitual to it. The strongest feeling of everyone was that Martin Derrick had been treated with injustice. He had been (wrested in his own house, and every man among them could realise the bitterness of such an insult to one's own hearthstone. He had been carried off to prison ; not been let out on bail as lie was before; and dark visions of the sufferings and indignities he must have gone through in Exeter gaol, filler the villagers minds. All the while he was an innocent and deeply injilted man; and then the question began to be asked—had he ever had fair play? So the farmers, all of whom in days gone by had more or less boycotted Martin Derrick, now one after another held out their hands to him. "We're uncommonly glad to see you safe home again, Mr. Derrick." - Hope you haven't suffered in your health from all you have gone through." . "You've been served shameful by the magistrates, and the whole lot of them -- "None of ,us are safe if this here sort of thing is to be let go on, innocent parties to be took up and sent to gaol !" , Martin tried to respond graciously, but these salutations caused extreme discomfort to the reserved and sensitive man. More was to come, however. Somehow the very hour of Martin's arrival home had become known in the village and as they came to a part where the road widened, and the whitesvashed WesleYan Chapel on the one side, and on the other Watkin's cottage, with "Devon Constabulary" painted above the doorway, and the principal shop, and the one humble little public-house of the village, near at nand, all gave importance to the spot—there stood a group of men and women, girls and boys, who as the well-known trap and brown horse came in sight, began to wave hats and handkerchiefs. "This is more than I had bargained for," said Martin with almost a groan. I wish we had driven round by the other road." " Ah, but it does them good, poor souls," replied Anne, gently. "They have a feeling that everybody has been unfair to you." - He was 'now forced to smile . and nod to the Nople as he drove past them—somewhat as if he had been made a king, very much against his will. Then a boy called out— Three cheers for Martin Derrick !" and so they hurrahed after him until he was vell out of hearing. And now they were away from the cottages, right out in the open solitary country, with the rolling purple brown waves of Dartmoor spreading oat before them' waves crested here and there with granite rocks. It was a. calm, grey, winter's day; the air came softly from the south-west, from the sea beyond Mount Edgecombe, just faintly visible in the far horizon. Martin drew a long breath of the fresh, sweet- scented air; he held his head a little higher, the colour came back to his wan cheeks, a look of deep content was in his eyes. "I don't think I ever knew before how much I cared fer every square inch of the_place," said he. "We have gone through a great deal together here, Anne, you and I, but we have been very happy together all the same, anti we will never leave Row Tor Farm if,we can help it." There was nothing unwelcome to Martin in the further greeting which awaited him as he drove lila to his own door. Richards and his wife in their Sunday bast, with beaming faces, stood. there to wels,ome the beloved y sung master. Eliza, who had not quite recovered the ordeal of giving evidence before the coroner and the magis- trate, kad vone for a week's holiday to her aunt's house at Plymouth. It Was happiness unspeakable to Msatia, to come back to his home ; to feel his freedon* in every breath he drew, to walk :shoat the familiar rooms, which were radiant with lirolight, mind with the last flowers of tins yea.r—oilrytill etnUlll4 an:l a few late roses. His own especial armchair wai drawn up to the parlour lire ; on the table the best-, white damask cloth was' spread, and it was la:len wit it what looked like a wedding feast, so ;sarnislied weSe the substantial dish en with flowers and evergreens. But before he would touch food, or seat himself by his own fireside, Martin said in a low voice to Antic: "I should like to see Mrs. Lawson awl thank hei kr all that she has done for you." lie did not yen tare to claim aay of Mrs. Laweon's kindness as in Waded for bluisolf.

BARON VON GRUNTSTEIN. PART SECOND. THE GHOST IS WARRANTED TO APPEAR IN THIS CHAPTER.

There was one peculiarity about old Baron yon Grun- stein—he had lost his memory. One day several years before, when the Baron was a stronger man .than we find him at the opening of this truthful story, he had ridden down from the castle to the lower then in that dare-devil style of his, and there had been an accident. The horse rolled over and over, and although half the time the Baron had been uppermost, this was small con- solation t. a man who was accustomed to he all the time on top. They picked him up. and a wild thrill of hope that he was killed had gone through the village, but the villagers, alas, were doomed to disappointment. The Baron recovered in every respect, and was as well as be- fore, with the one exception that his memory Was en- tirely. gone. This turned out to be a great blessing to his dependents, for if they could only stave off a row for a little thee, the Baron forgot all about it. The old butler, who was almost as great a thief as the Baron himself, had been dismissed time and again, but he never went, and when he appeared next day as usual the Baron had forgotten all about the trouble. Now, if I.were to scold and abuse my servants, and . .
Lccepted, nd

throw carving knives and such utensils at them, pinning them to the oaken wall now and then, they would arise in a body and leave me. They would give me warning. But when a person is a Baron they seem to stand a great deal from him, and they lack the proper respect for him if he don't occasionally knock some of them down. But then, you see, there are more perquisites to be picked up about an old castle than there are about your residence or mine. So the old Baron's servants stuck to him and trembled, and he had little trouble, except now an 4 then surgery bill, when he happened to throw the carving knife straighter than usual, and pinned a helion to the wall. After the events narrated in the last chapter the Baron went to Berlin and had a good time for three months, and then the gout jumped on him, and he left the giddy pleasures of that city, and came back to recruit in the castle by the Rhine. He always liked to spend Christmas in his ancient fortress. You see, I have to lug Christmas into this story somehow, because it is written for the Christmas number, and the publishers would be disappointed if they found that Christmas was not mentioned somewhere in the yarn. Christmas hasn't anything .to do with the thrilling events that I have narrated, and that tam about to narrate, but I can't risk censure merely for a little thing like that, so in comes Mr. Christmas dragged by the collar. This is a Christmas story, and I don't propose thee that fact shall be fo gotten. Well, on Christmas Eve, there were' unusual prepara- tions at the Grunstein Castle. There was no gas or electric light plant in the ancient building,so the verger, or whatever he was called, had to get a step-ladder and light the thousands of wax candles that were in the great candelabra of the mammoth dining-hall. The end of the Leader was in the habit of slipping on the polished floor of the cestle, and many a nasty fall the old man got before the hall was ablaze with light, but at last his task was done, although not without the use of a great deal of very bad ,German language which! don't propose to set down on this page. The old Baron was seated at the held of the table looking as fierce as ever ; more so, in fact, for his game leg was upon another chair in a great bundle, which showed what a good time he had had in Berlin. The Baron dined alone. It may be said that he was rather unpopular with the neighbouring gentry. Some murders that the Baron had committed, years before, seemed to have engendered a prejudice against him. Not that his neighbours objected to murder, hut they thought it ought to be done deftly and unobtrusively. They con- sidered it bad form to club a man in the public highway, or to throw him over the battlements into the village, and thus muss up the streets that had to be kept tidy at the public expense. So the old Baron dined alone. He never cared for company anyhow, and fastidious guests objected to have a joint of meat flung at them when they got the better of the Baron in an argument on the Irish question. Just as the boar's head was being brought in with groat ceremony, the Baron noticed two strangers ap- proach from the outer door unannounced. "Who are those people ?" shouted the Baron, grasping the carving knife ; at which the menials unconsciously flung up their arms to guard their heads. "How dare you allow anyone to come in here unannounced when I am about to begin dinner ?" The menials looked at each other and turned pale. The old Baron, they thought, was losing his head. There wag no one in the room as far as they knew. l'cobedy, however, liked to contradict the Baron. The last one who had done so was still in the hospital. Meanwhile, the two strangers calmly approached the table, and without.waiting for an invitation sat down, one on each side of the Baron. At this the old Baron was in a fine rage. Without a word of warning, he flung the carving knife at the man pn the left hand side of him and that weapon went through the stranger's body and sunk in the back of the old oaken chair. "Very well thrown, Baron,"said the ghost with a thin smile, "shy the fork at my friend, if you like. If it amuses you, pray don't consult our feelings at all. We don't mind it. I fear you done recollect me. Baron." The Baron gasped and turned very red. He tugged at his neck-cloth, and seemed to choke. Then he gulped down a flagon of wine, and said: "Really, I don't think I have the honour of your ac- quaintance." "My name is Liberey W. Palladium," said the ghost, "and I come from Chicago. Great city, Baron. If you ever come West you ought to take in Chicago. Perhaps you remember that I called here one night, and you left me up in that airy bedroom of yours, on the tower. My bones, I believe, are there yet.' "I'm very sorry," stammered the Baron, "but really the circumstance slipped my memory. I have a dim recollection of the matter. Since you came in I seem to remember things clearer than I used to. lam really very sorry about that tower mishap." Oh, don't mention it," said the ghost easily. "I would have called on you sooner, but I did not know your Ber- lin address, and so had to wait until you came home. I want to get back to Chicago to spend the holidays." "Then you don't intend to remain in this country ?'' said the Baron with a feeling of relief. "No, sir. This country is too slow for me. I expect to have a lot of fun with the bo.t s when I get back to Chicago. They never went Much on the ghost business out there, and I expect to give.them some kinks in that line. I understand that it is considered the proper thing that I should stay here and haunt this castle, and es- pecially the tower." • "I hope you won't put yourself to any inconvenience on that account," hastily remarked tbe Baron. "Oh, I won't; you bet. I got a substitute. You see, during our war, if a fellow was drafted into the army, he could always get a substitute, and I proposed this in the 'ghost realm. It struck them as a new thing, and I was told that if I could get a substitute to attend to this old castle, I could go to Chicago or anywhere else. So I just dropped round to introduce try substitute to you, and then I'm off for Chicago." " And is this—this—gentleman your substitute ?" muttered the Baron, uneasily. The other ghost, who was a most hideous person, gave a diabolical leer at the Baron, which made him shudder. The ghost of Mr. P. said: " Allow me to introduce you ; Baron, this is your Lost Memory. I found him wandering about in space. and offered him nice quarters in the castle. He and said he was very familiar with both you h. .11e castle. That, in fact, he was your own Lost Memory. He thinks that you and he will have some pleasant moments chatting over old times."
wi • '4,l`zy
RY

"It is very good of him," gasped the old Baron, but. really I don't want to have anything to do with him. I would prefer thdt you remain, Mr. Palladium, and I cant say that I like Americans either. Still I would prefer you.'

. - "It may seem strange 0 you, Baron, but notwith- atanding the hospitality I have nit ,with within these walls, ;have had all I can stand OE khe'Castle.orunltein. NO; yotir Memory and you will' have to fight it out. I can't stay. Well, good-night, Baron. I wish you a-merry Christmas." •

At this the Memory laughed a hideous laugh that made the old Baron tremble like one of his own menials. , The ghost of Mr. P. shook hands with the Memory, nodded to the Baron, who sat there in a state of stupe- faction and withdrew.

Well, old man," said the Memory, "it's some little time since you and I worked together. By the way, how's your brother " Hus-s-s-s-sh!" whispered the Baron, turning pale. "Don't speak so loud. lies dead, you know." "So he is. I remember how it came about, too. You-.-"
"For the sake of-Heaven," screamed the Baron, "don't talk of these things , "You forget," said the Memory, " that no one am hear, me but yourself." •

‘ I aiii,glad of that," replied the Baron, in a ;gone of relief,‘ as he looked around at ,his frightened servants, who were huddled together at one end of the room. they csaild only hear the Baron talking, and they could see only the Baron there, and as telephones were not in vogue at that time in Germany, and as they had never beheld the spectacle of a man talking to an invisible person through a telephone, they did not know what to make of it. If they had been acquainted with the tele- phone, the old Baron carrying on a conversation, one end of which they did not hear, might not have seemed so strange; as it was, they thought he was crazy. The old valet went gingerly up to the oaken chair in whicb the carving-knife stuck, and pulled it out. He dropped on one knee, and begged the Baron to throw it at some- ' body, then it would seem like old times. It nearly broke the old retainer's heart to see. the Baron lay the knife aside and mournfully shake his head. "I am very glad," said the Baron to his 113emor1, "that what you say is only heard by me. It would be rather awkward otherwise." "Yes," said the demon with a repulsive grin. "But what is of more account, I can make you say just what I please, and people will pay more attention to what a Baron would say than to the words of a spectre." At this the Baron began to feel uneasy again. "For instance," went on the Memory," just apologise to your servants for your treatment of them." '- Before the Baron knew wnat he was about be had applogised, and the servants nearly fell down in their astonishment. "They don t deserve to be apologised to," mild the Memory, "for they have robbed you right and left. I merely made you do so in order to make the work I have cut out for you the easier. Now, to-morrow. y9tt must hunt out your nephew Gottlieb von Grinostem,. who is, as you very well know, the real heir to this castle and your wealth. I believe be sells tickees down at the office of the Rhino steamers, on a salary of twelve marks a week. You have never done anything for bun. Well, you will have to make over all this property te him, That will be a nice Christmas gift, eh, old man? "I will into. do it I" cried the Baron, bringing down his fist on the table somewhat after his old w'yle• at which his servants began to take heart again. "Oh, won't you ?" said the Memory sneeringly. "No, I won't. I'll die first." "Very well. That will be just as you, please. Then" to-morrow I will make you confess all about your murder of his father, and where you have hidden the papers that show to whom the estate belongs. A fine figure you would make on the scaffold, Baron. Isee you are changing your mind. Well, just as you please- It don't make any difference to me, except that the sooner you shuffle off the sooner I will be released from attending you. You musn't think that I yearn for your company, Baron." So next day the Baron, very much subdued, went down to the village and found his nephew. The offices of the Rhine Co. were closed during the winter season, and the young man was very glad indeed to get a per- manent situation as a German Baron. He was a kind young man, and did what he could for his old uncle. It was said to him that his uncle had been a crutl man, but young Gottlieb remarked that that did not matter —he was his uncle—he could not forget that. So when navigation opened, the kind-hearted young man used his influence at the shipping offices of the nine steamers, and he got the old Baron the place of ticket clerk at twelve marks a week. When people praised him ' for this. he magnanimously waved his hand and said.. "What would you? I have but done my duty."

In writing the foregoing story it will be noticed that I have studiously refrained from running in the original German in the conversations; of course, all the con- versations took place in German, as well as in German 7 I have confined myself ta..Anglish,,for two reaf,nerfw the first place, many of my readers may not know German language; in the second place. I-do not knoif word of it myself.—From the Christmas Number of ' Detroit Free Press.

1710 nett';', -'. M.. °ND-AY- - Nra-zr. .1-7 i-demonstration held in honour of Mr. Gladstone was of a most interest,- character. More than 1,000 members of the Graribal- . n Association went to the lodgings of the great Eng- la statesman. They arrived just as he was leaving the use with his daughter. Be was at once surrounded .1., a large crowd of sympathisers, who repeatedly burst Lto elks of "Long live Gladstone." "Lor'e* live Ire- 'ad." Subsequently Mr. Gladstone receiveda depute- ' t,...1°13, and an address of welcome was read, in which he 1 spoken of as the representative of a generous ion, which had welcomed the Italian exiles when eY were driven from their own country. The address ~.also contained an allusion to the good effected by the wse, stablishment of the Irish Church, by the Education ~_"act, sod by the Irish Land Acts. It gratefully recalled fe spirited oratory of the ex-Premier and his courage 'a denc*ncing the tyranny of the Bourbons. From that rnvment Mr. Gladstone was enshrined in every Italian heart and in the memory of every European democracy. The address concluded with these stirring 'Words s--" The glorious work is not yet finished, but it r ill be worthily crowned when a measure of Home Rule "er Ireland. which is desired by all the Liberals of the new generation, becomes law." Mr. Gladstone. in reply, said that he had come to Italy for rest and quiet, but that he was much touched by the sympathy of the Italian democracy. lie assured them of his love for Italy. and said that he always desired to be useful to their country. The right hon. gentleman seemed in excellent health, although his voice was rather weak. To-day a representatlve of the Syndic. who is ill, called on Mr. Gladstone in the name of the city of Florence. Signer Puccini, a senator of the Imperial Parliament and presi- dent of a leading political association, presented an ad- dress recalling, the great services rendered by me Glad- stone to Italy, and expressing the hope and conviction that before long the cause of Ireland would triumph. .

A catalogue of the great/public disaaters of last year would, remarks a Yorkshire paper, begin and end with calamities in connection with the drama. In January occurred the panic caused by a false alarm of fire in the Hebrew Dramatic' Club, Spitalfields, when seven- teen persons were trodden to death, and the very close of the year saw the destruction by fire of the Grand Theatre, Islington, at which happily no human life was lost. But between these two events had occurred the appalling calamity caused by the burning of the theatre at Exeter, by which over 130, people lost their lives. That terrible holocaust has not been without its good fruits, for the authorities everywhere are now looking closely to the safety of the public in all Once of public amusement, so as to reduce the possibility .4 such events to .a minimum. The record of rail-, way travelling for the year is marred by the deplor- able • affair at ,Hexthorpe. Dangers at sea have been exemplified abundantly. The first month of the year saw the loss ,of the British emigrant ship, the Kapunda, along Withmearly three hundred lives. Then" there was the wreck of the Brighton and South Coast Railway steamer, the Victoria, with the loss ef twenty lives; the Wasp is believed to have gone down with all on board; the City of Montreal was burned at, sea,.bni without loss of life; and the terrible sinking of the Dutch emigrant ship, the W. A. Scholten,:is still pain- fully fresh in the mind. The colliery explosions in the Rhondda Valley in February; at Udsten, in Lanark- shire, in May, when 73 lives were lost ;'-and in the Walker Pit, near Newcastle, in October, will place the number of deaths from this cause higher than the 116 registered for DM,. But with the New Year comes in the Mines Regulation Act, Which is confidently looked to for the diminishing of such causes of danger and death. _
EXTRAORDINARY SHOOTING CASE.'

Great excitement and consternation was caused in- Ramsgate on Sunday night by the conduct of a man named Allen William Richardson. At about 20 minutes' -past nine o'clock he was walking in George-street when he suddenly accosted a young woman with the words, "You're the girl !" and immediately fired two shots from a revolver at her. Fortunately both shots missed her. -Passing on Richardson met a member of the Salvation Army, and fired two shots at him. Again the shots missed; but the man had a narrow escape, the bullets whizzing closely past his head. By this time a considerable crowd, attracted by the sound of firing had gathered, aid pursued Richardson, who fled at great speed. His- pursuers, however, gained upon him, and finding him- self close pressed he suddenly turned, and again fired at the foremost of the crowd. The shot struck a lad named Pillow, who fell on the pavement. He was I immediately taken to a surgeon, and was afterwards re- moved to the Infirmary. A policeman named Sandoin joined in the chase, but Richardson escaped to his house 'in Ducan-road. He was next seen at an upper window with a double-barrelled gun in his hand. Hardly had ht. shown himself when he discharged both barrels at the crowd below, one shot striking a young man named Moody in the head, while another struck a potman named Fox. Both the sufferers were removed to the Infirmary, where they remain. After the lapse of some time, 10 or 12 policemen arrived and •broke into the I house. After a severe struggle Richardson was arrested and removed to the police-station. The prisoner, who is 37 years of age, is a man of independent means. At his house were found two guns, two large pistols, and' a revolver, with a quantity of ammunition. .

DEATHS OF EMINENT MEN IN 1887. The most important name in the obituary of the year is that of Lord Iddesleigh, better known as Sir Stafford Nortlicote, whose Scrupulous fairness of mind and un-; ruffled geniality of temper in the trying pbsition of leader; of the House of Common had won him the affectionate mud of men of all parties. Lord Lyons the Most ac- complished and experienced of English diplomatists, had retired from the Paris gmbassy, Where he was succeeded by Lord Lytten,tjust before he was struck down by his last illness. Among others well known in the political or social world of England who have passed away during the year may be mentioned Mr. Beresford-Hope, Mr. Newdegate, Sir William M'Arthur, and Mr. Itylands, who had been so long familiar figures in Parliament% Lord Wolverton, the most faithful of Mr. Gladstone's fol- lowers; Lord and Lady Dalhousie, cut off by a strange and sad fate within a few days of ono another; General Valentine Baker, best known as Baker Pashto, the rank he had won in the Turkish and Egyptian armies; Sir Joseph Whitworth, a great name in the world of industry and invention; Sir Philip Wodeimuse, Sir Ashley Eden, Sir Henry Gordon, Sir Robert Montgomery, Sir John and Mr. Justice Lawson, who had served the State wellin different spheres of duty; Jenny Lind, in her day the most renowned of operatic singers; Sir George Madarren, a life-long labourer in the muse of musical education ; Mr, Thrirtg, head master of Upping- ham; Serjetint Ballantine Lady Braseey, Professor Spencer Baynes, Mr. Mackonochie, of St. Alban'. Holborn; Mrsh Craik, the author of "J.' a Halifax ;" Mr. Richard Jefferies,• the author of " Tile Ganiekeeper at Home ;" Sir Geory Burrows, the Nestor of the medical profession; Mr. Palgrave Simpson. the dramatist; and Archdeacon M'Gettigan, the Roman Catholic Primate of Ireland. Abroad the list of eminent men who have passed away during the year is a scanty rine. In Michael Katkoff, the famous editor of the Mos- cato Gazette, Russia parted with the very embodiment of her national spirit and a power in the Stateecarcelv second to the Czar himself. France loat M. Raoul Duval a Conservative who had frankly accepted the Republic Admiral .Taureguiberry, and M. Paul Feral, a veteran romancist ; Germany, Herr Krupp, the founderef The vast ironworks and gun factories at Essen, and Profes- sor Range, the theologian; Italy, Signor Depretis. one of the ablest of the statesmen of the Monarchy, And Card ihal Jaeobini, the Papal Secretary of State; Belgium, M. Gallait, the pdinter ; the United States, Mr. Tilden; the Democratic candidate for the Presidency in 18760 and Mr. Washburne, formerly Minister in Paris. Langiewiez, the leader of the Poles in the insurrection of 1863, and Father Beekx, formerly "General" of the Jesuits,...eiti hardly be described as belonging to any country. •

THE PAPAL JUBILEE.—LEO 11.11. BIOGRAPHICAL SKEI'CIi • Leo XIII. fills a mighty part in the world's history. s hot only because he occupies the historic throne of th, I Popes, but also because he has been endowed with Fou- -1 derful mental capacity. He was brilliant as a student. I energetic as a simple priest, far-seeing as a diplomatist, and zealous and vigilant as a Bishop and a Cardinal, but it is as the Supreme Ruler of the Church that the splen- did qualities of his mind have shone forth. He rose to the opportunities which occurred:throughout his' life. and when c,n took the position of successor of St. Peter sod spiritus father of 225.00,000 of human belugs.. ihis wisdom and his power of dealing with difficult ques- ,tions appeared in the fullest and most highly developed form. Joachim Vincent Peed was born on the 2n-i 1810, at Carpineto, of Anna Proeperi end Count ;Louis Peed, and' was the Youngest of six children. TI, Icountryin - widths he passed his-childhood-is Wild fill,' picturesque, and lathy therefor be said to be a mew murse for a child of lofty sentiments. The people are, a a rule, simple in their habits, and fervid in their pity . , The parents of the future Pope, who belonged to th. Italian nobility, and were possessed of that devotion te the Church which is such a•glettious trait ie Uiet eharac 'tarot the true Italian' Instilled into the minds' of tie+ -children an isrdent lovefor religion, end a desire to farm the examples of Christian fortitude and dm rity with whist •the history of Italy abounds. Josef Vincent, it w. soon discovered, had even in his earliest years, a recep- tive mind, and profited by the excellent lesson., he re- ceived. When he had reached the age of eight„Toechbe Vincent was sent to the Jesuit College at Viterbo. le this adittirable school he spent six rears. He showed a taste for study, and a special aptitude for the sicquieit len sof classical knowledge, and under the charee of the 'Jesuit Fathers, the beauties of his own mother tongue and the ancient Latin which it succeeded, were ably on folded to 'hint In 1824, after the death of his mother. be proceeded to the Eternal City, in which he was dos. tined to become one day the central figure. Ile reside••,' with hie uncle at the Unfti Palace, and attended th. Roman College. The institution had just been restored_ to the Jesuits, and they installed therein a brilliant 'band 61 teachers who did honour to the , Church by their 'indefatigable labours. He was at once a quick and assiduous student. His SUCC4SA in com- petition VMS most marked. Ile carried off prizes for Latin composition, Greek, physics, and ehernistry and underwent with singular credit two public exami- nations at the Roman Coliege and in the Saprenti Hiliver- sity. Of legal and diplomatie knowledge he acquired an ample store at- the Academy of Noble Ecclesiastics. In 1837, when he was not more than twenty-six rears of age, Gregory XVI. appointed him a Prelate of his House- hold and aeferenday Of the Segnatum. Some months afterwards—in December, 1837—Mgr. Pecci was, raised to the priesthood, and celebrated Its first Mass in the chapel of St. Stanislaus, Koetka, at the Church of St. Andrea on the Quirinal, being assisted by his brother, the Rev. Joseph Peed, then a Jesuit and now a prince of the Church. In February, 184 he was entrusted with the govemors.hip of Benevento, a pro- vince which at that time was the prey of lawless bends. Brigands ravaged the country, levying blackmail, and terrorising the population. Mgr. Pecci took in band resolutely the work of reform. 'He was stern and unbending in punishing the brigands and repressing lawlessness. High and low were equally made to feel that they would not be permitted to disturb the peace. In the course of a few years the disgrace of brigandage was thus wiped out completely from the province. But the action of the governor was not all repressive. He was kind and tender to the poor, and showed genuine zeal for the improvement of the comp try, keeping the necessity of progress steadily in view. Mgr. Peed was chosen as delegate to Spoleto, but Pope Gregory XVI., knowing his capacity for dealing with difficult situations, decided, a few day's after that ap- pointment had been made, to transfer lm to the more important post of delegate to Perugia. Umbria, of : which this ancient and interesting city is the capital, 'was at that time the seat of much discontent. Secret societies were flourishing, the faith was growing weaker, trade' was languishing, and the people were weighed 'down with imposts_ Monsienor Pecci resolved to .bring about a thorough change,. and, by energy and vigilance, he fully succeeded in his object. The gaols Were soon absolutely empty, and the people prosperous and • contented. When Gregory XVI. came tei visit them, in company with the Delegate, he Was ac- corded a reception which could not be surpassed for cordiality.. • In the early part of 1843, at the age of 33, he was called to that eminent position in which he proved 'the sountinesa'of the opinions already formed of his diplomatic talents, and exhibited to the gaze of Europe his high statesmanlike qualifies. In Januaryrof that year he was named Apostolic Nitncio at the Court of Brussels. The dignity otTittalar Atchbishop was oonferred on him, the See of liatriietta being assigned to hint On the 19th February he received his episcopal consecration in the church of San Lorenzo, on the Viminal Hill, at the hands of Cardinal Lambruschini. In the ensuing month Arch- bishop Pecci was at his post. There was then, as thereis now,a, bitter strife between the Catholics and the so-called Liberals 'of the country, one, of the chief objects alined at by the latterlbeing the secularisation of education. Mgr. Pecci, without outstepping the limits of action laid -do-wit for official dipiorsatistsg-displayed a seem inter- est, in the cause of education. ,The reat controversy, over Brussels University raged most furiously. The Archbishop acted with conSummate prudence, taking care not to accentuate the differences which already, existed, but, at the same time, heartily aiding that educational movement amongst the Catholics which has given to the Catholic University of Louvain the fore- most posit t amongst the great centres of learning the Continent. He paid a visit to tbs.:, fameus institu- tion, then, es now, regarded as the hOpc and pride of Catholic Belgium, and -vas received with the most. marked hononri. By King Leopold and the distinguished personages of his Court, the Nuncio was held in Ole highest esteem. He spoke French with such purity riC accent that the • King was wont to remark that he ebvays mistook the Archbishop for a Frenchman. It was, therefore, with universal regret that the TIC,VS AVMS received in Brussels and throughout Belgium tied the Nuncio had been appointed to it poqitiiiii—ibe lii,hopric of Ferucia—the acceptance of which would compel him to resign his appointment and wiH Ore w from the Belgian capital. The Xing was particularly kind on his !ea,•••tasing. He decorated him with ti., 'rope; it the Order of Leopold, and forwarded t I fittly Tither a letter in which he bore testiimee fa. hi ability; soundness of judgment and sense of d Sty. Mgr. Pecci left Brussels in April. 1845. It was at this time that he paid a month's visit to England, and re- csived an invitation to tho Court of Queen Victoria. Speaking French fluently, and a little English, he had little dif6eutty in making himself acquainted • with the ledding characteristics of the Most remarkable monu- ments in the metropolis. When the Archbishop, reached It once,— Greg76i7 XVI. lay on his death-bed. The deep regret which he experienced at the loss of his friend and spiritual father was counterbalanced by the happiness of seeing another dignitary with whom he had already been brought into kindly relations Cardinal Mastai-Ferretti —placed on the Throne of Peter. As first Bishop of Perugia. Cardinal Pecci entered into possession of his See on the 26th July„ 1846, and for the long period of thirty-two years het governed that diocese. There were three points to which he devoted special attention. It was his earnest wish that the clergy of his diocese should never lay themselve9 open to the charge of inactivitv: He was anxious to place witliin the reach of those destined for the services of the Church the means of securine such an education as would put them fully abreast of the times, and enable, them to give a ready answer to all who attacked the truths of the Christian religion. And he desired particularly to mint out the principles by the adoption of which the difficulties prevailing be- tween labour, and capital might be solved. The revolutionary and anti-Christian spirit which was fostered by Mazzini and Garibaldi permeated Umbria after the Piedniontese occupation. The evils under which the Chtirch had to suffer were pretty much the same as they are at the present day. In the year 1853 Archbishop Peed was proclaimed is Cardinal of the Order of Priests by the late Pope Pius IX., and the event was celebrated with rejoicing not only in his own diocese bid , likewise in the Eternal City, where his zeal and ability were well known. Amongst the many distinguished personages who called upon the Archbishop to tender their congratulations was the present Crown Prince of Germany. Another event which gave joy to the Catho- lics of his diocese was his Silver Jubilee, or the 25th anniversary of his appointment to the See. In Sep- tember, 1877; the Cardinal took up his residence in Rome, ' In succession to the Camarlengo. Cardinal de Angelis.

ir4 .14stied limiter a few' math; plWreitar? the 7th January, 1878, the great Pontiff, Pope Pins IX., who struggled so bravely with adversity and who by his ardent love of his spiritual children, endeared him- self to them in a special manner, passed to his eternal rest. The end of his glorious career was saddened by thigkening miseries and the vision of dark, overhanging ckmds. The Piedmonteee invaders had succeeded in arresting from him the immemorial patrimony of the Supreme Pontiffs. They had brought with them the scum of the Italian population into the Eternal City, and they imprianned the august ruler of the Church in the palace of the Vatican. The revolutionary societies which were 'et work throughout Huron° sympathised with their brother revolutionists in Italy, and the Holy Father found himself opposed and misrepresented on all points. It can easily be conceived how terrible was the re- • sponsibility whieh devolved upon his successor. It Is no exaggeration to say that at the date of his election nearly all the Governments of Europe looked upon the Holy See with hostile gaze. 'lle Cardinals met in the Pauline Chapel on the 18th February, and took the oath prescribed by the Canons. After the customary ceremonies they were installed in their respective cells. Next morning, after Mass, they breakfasted in their cells. They then proceeded to the election of the new Pontiff. In the first ballot Cardinal Pecci received twente-three votes; Cardinal Bilio. eleven; Cardinal Fraochi, four: and Cardinal Pane- [Wane°, four. The other votes were distributed amongst a number of the Cardinals. Owing to a slight infer- raality—one of the Cardinals having, contrary to the regulations, affixed to his paper a real bearing the mark of his dignity—the first ballot was declared void. In the second, thirty-eight votes out of sixty-one were riven to Cardinal Pecci. As the votes wiiich he had received did not amount to two-thirds, &nether ballot Lecanie necessary. This took place next day, when his I'minence, Cardinal Plead, was elected Pope by 44 votes' I out of 82. Cardinal Peeci, on being asked what name he I would llSRUElManawered that lie would tAke the name of Leo XIII. The Cardinalatial ring having been removed and the ring of the Fisherman ran en, cardinal ceterini, the senior Cardinal-Deacon, then announced the election of the Pope from the Loggia on the facade of St. Peter's: The news was received with shouts of joy,•and, whilst I the hells of the city rang out merry peals, the anti- ( hrietian Radicalism of Rome seemed for the moment ea:l-existent. On the 22nd February. hi Holiness ierieived in audience the ambassadors ot France, Spain. l'ortugahand A W4tria,and then followed /1 url i meat to a vast I number of Whet i 11S. who tendered their congratulations. The impressive ceremony of coronation way performed it the Sistine Chanel, on Sunday, the 3rd March, the fardinal-Defteen placitig the 'flare on the head of the [ venerable Pontiff.* and saying in a loud voice, "Receive the Tiara, (servant...mid with three crowns, and know that 3 ou are the father of princes and Hugs, the ruler of the world, the Vicar ri,virtkof our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom e honour end gl.ry for gver and ever. Amen." At the close of tins cerenattny. ill- Heti!~ Imparted the Triple Benedic- t ion, and then received on address from the Sacred College. In the Brief which he addressed to the Emperor of Ger- many, announcing his accession, his Holiness] Appealed to the magnanimity of that monarch for the restoration et peace, and the tranquillity of conscience to his catholic subjects. The negotiations which were the ooneequeneess of that appeal have had, as Ku Europe now recognises. the happiest results. In the early (lays of his Pontificate Leo XIII., by restoring .the Catholic Hierarchy in Scotland, fulfilled a desire which his predecessor, Pope Phis IX., had entertained for some time , previous to his death. Another act of his Holinees. which is of special interest to the Catholics of these islands, is that by which he •rtiaed his Eminence Cardinal Newman —asserts)* et senora- I ;J'e comes—to the dignity of the purple; and his name is still further endeared to the Catholics of England by its egnciatioct with the Beatification of the English Martyrs. I (Inc of the most striking" aspects of the policy of Leo XIII. is its applicability to the present time. He has studied the past with the mind of one who is thoroughly alive to the present. John Sheehy, who tried to save Geary. was bitten on the fingers, with the result that blood poisoning has since set in, and his life is despaired of.
