div.head: STORM AND LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: STORM AND LOSS OF LIFE.

A heavy westerly gale blew over the Isle of Man on Tuesday night. The schooner Daisy, of Chester, was running into Douglas Bay, for shelter, when she 4truck on the Conister Rock. The lifeboat was launched, an the Crew of three men and a boy rescued. At high water the schooner was toWed off the rock, but sank almost immediately. The lives of nine men on board her at the time were seriously , imperilled, but all were eventually rescued. The schooner Lyra, of Port St. Mary, in trying to enter Port St. Mary harbour struck on the Carrick Rock. The Port Erin and Castletown lifeboats were dragged overland and launched, and the former suc- ceeded in rescuing three men. The captain, Fran- cis Petherick, of Port St. Mary, was washed over- board and drowned. A heavy gale also prevailed over almost the whole of Ireland on Tuesday night' and on Wednesday. A large vessel was driven ashore near Waterford Harbour, and a tugboat went out to try and rescue the crew. The tugboat, how- /ever, was unable to approach the vessel, and the captain states that while close to the wreck, he saw the crew put off in a boat. The sea dashed the boat on to. tbe rocks, and he was convinced that its oc- eupantsi at least ten in number, were all drowned. A later account states that the barque wrecked on Wednesday, was the Alfred Snow, of ThomasT 1, tone, from San Francisco. AU hands, numbering thirty, wde drowned. The body of the master, named Willy% has been washed ashore. Owing to the heavy weatherin the Channel several Atlantic liners were considerably delayed.

div.head: BOLTON THEATRE DESTROYED
div.p: BOLTON THEATRE DESTROYED

• BY FIRE. * SUSPECTED INCENDIARISM. About four o'clock on Wednesday morning, fire broke out at the Bolton Theatre Royal. and in lees then an hour the building was destroyed. Mr. J. F. Elliston, the lessee, had this year produced the pan- tomime of "Blue- Beard," ancht prAmised ;to be most suecessful. There were two performances on Tuesday, the house being crowded both afternoon and evening. Everything was left safe.at midnight, and the first intimation of the fire was given by the police. The theatre is in a thickly-populated neighbourhood, and great difficulty was experienced 'in rescuing the inmates of several houses adjoining. 'At a blitcher's shop in tie vicinity, the onthouses were destroyed, and four sheep and a cow burned to death. All the artistes properties at the theatre were burned, the Korrie musical troupe alone losing .£2OO. The theatre was 'fitted with Grinnell's pa- tent, sprinklers and all the latest appliances, but burglarious. implements were found at the office entrance, and the valve tap connected with the sprinklers was tempered with, so that they could net operate: The leather strap which forms part of an ingenious mechanical contrivance regulating the inflow of water from the main had, as a matter of fact, been cut in two places. These circum- stances Point to incendiarism The Bolton Fire Brigade succeeded, with much difficultyin'eonfining, the fire to the theatre, but the flames were not ex- tinguished until ten o'clock in the 'morning, by which time the whole of the theatre building, in- cluding the scenic artist's room at the, back, was% completely razed to the ground. One hundred and eighty persons are thrown out of employ 4 ment by the disaster. The building is partially insured.

Elliston says he his no doubt that the fire is the work of an incendiary, probably from wilful malice or from carelessness on the part of some one intent on robbing the premises. The lessee's 'office was broken into, but two safes within it *ere un- injured, and none of the papers were. disturbed. ;A chisel, pickaxe, and bar of iron were found on *6 floor. The door had been forced open with a titf which had been brought from the stage, which 155 at the opposite end of the theatre. A bunch of keyi had also been removed in like manner. Two of the members of the Grand Theatre Company, London, who were to haie commenced an engagement with Mr. Elliston, on Wednesday, had not deposited any portion of their wardroke within the theatre, but they will lose lueratire employment.. All the in- struments of the band, including a piano onstink 100 guinea, and a violin 200 years old, were dest troyed. Four tanini of oxy-hydrogen, used in the pantomime, exploded with a terrific report.-; It 'is estimated that the loss will amount to not less than £15,000: The last tire of this kind in 13olton was when the Temple Opera House, in Dawes- street, was burned ,down, on the night of the 16th April, 1882, the damige done then being estimated at .ElO.OOO. . " A fund has been opened. in Bolton for the relief of the actors thrown out of engagements by the destruction of the theatre. The belief that 'the' disaster was caused by an incendiary s confirmed by a statement ot a constable who was told a few days ago that the proprietor of the theatre would catch it hot within a week for supporting the authorities in maintaining extra police in the town during the recent strike disturbances. div.head: MR. WILFRID BLUNT ANT) HIS APPEAL.
div.p: MR. WILFRID BLUNT ANT) HIS APPEAL.

On Sunday, Mr: Wilfrid Blunt, Lady Anne Blunt, Mr. Evelyn, M.P., and Tle MacDermott. arrived.at Rirr. They were met at the railway 'station by a number of people with the town band. An address from the towns- people was presented by the Rev. Denis Sheehan, and the party proceeded to the parochial house, where they were entertained by the priests of the town. Great ex- citement was created by the arrival at the railway sta- tion. of Mr. David heelly. M.P.. in prison dress. The people pressed through the escort of police to shako hands with the prisoner, hut there was no conflict, good temper being maintained on both sides.• On Tuesday, at. Portumna, Mr. Wilfrid Blunt and Lady Anne Blunt were presented by Mr. Marcell with an aildress of symyathy from the Colchester Liberals. In his reply, Mr. Blunt said that there were no doubt persons in Dubli n Castle who knew what would be the issue •of his appeal, but no matter what punishment would be, inflicted upon him, it would not prevent him from doing again ivhat be had done. The hearing of Mr. Wilfrid Blunt's appeal against the decision of Messrs. Dillon and Me.Sheehy, resident magi- strates. who under the Crimes Act sentenced him to two months' imprisonment for obstructing the police in the discharge of their duty, at Wolidford, on the 23rd Octo- ber, was fixed to commence on Tuesday, at Portumna, before Mr. T. IL Rice Henn, Considesation judge, Galway. The court did not sit until 11 30, and ordinary business was pretvefiecl with first. • '

Mr. Atkinson, for the Crown In his opening.statementu announced to take place, at-iWoteelthrd,- on the 23rd -October, under the auSpi&S of The English Rome Rule Union, was pro- ciaiwied. Mr. Blunt., however, attended, and resisted the police, when they attempted to remove him from the platform. On the 16th, a week or so previously, :a. meeting had been held at Woodford at midnight hut the proceedings -at that meeting were not relevant- and till that Mr. Blunt had to answer for was his allegtd resistance to the police in the execution of theieduty on the 23rd October. • . - The Consideration Judge held that the previous meet- ing was vital, as showing the state of the surrounding ootiutry, and as bearing on the question of the legality of the meeting of the 23rd. Mr. Atkinson said he intended to show that the latter. meeting was an adjournment of the previous meeting. The MaeDermott protested that if this -course was pursued, he would insist on opening up the whole Irish question, and the investigation wonld last a fortnight. Eridonce was called on behalf of the police to prove the attempt to hold a meeting at Woodford, and to the resistance offered by. Mr. Blunt when removed from platform. The ease was ultimately adjOurnad.
tho

The hearing of the appeal was continued on Wednes- day, in a crowded court at Portumna. Several police witnesses spoke not only of the proceedings at Woodford pn October 23rd, but of the character of the midnight meetings on the previous Sunday, and of Ow general condition of the district. The case was again ad- journed. On Thursday Mr. Byrne, divisional magistrate, was examined. He said that if the meeting had not been proclaimed he would not have dispersed it. For the ap- pellat the Secretary of the English Home Rule Union was called, and he stated that Mr. Blunt was the dele- gate of that association, which bad nothing to do with the National League. The case was not concluded.

The two thousandth consecutive sermon by the Rev. .C. H. Spurgeon, entitled, "Healing by the Stripes of :Jesus," has been published. That a preacher should have issued a weekly sermon without intermission for the long period of 33 years is probably a fact unprecedented in the literature of• any country.

Sir Samuel Griffith, the Queensland Premier, has pro- pesed to invite Lord Wolseley to visit Australia to in. apect the military force and advise upon the defences of the various colonies. The Colonial Governments are now -cs-insidering the proposal. It is understood that Lord Wolseley would accept the invitation. The unionigts decline to work with the accommodators at this factory, but it is anticipated that the difficulty will be arranged by making separate shops. - - • • "Stu:Yr" Boors FOR POLICRMRW.—The police of Leeds are no longer to herald their approach to the midnight prowler, the burglar, and the industrious purloiner of forgotten triffes,.by the heaviest and loudest-speaking boots that it is poseihte to purchase, as the Chief Con- stable has directed that in tuture they shall be shod with what is known as time a silent" boot, and has given an order for between 400 and 500 pairs.

Suicror. OF A BOOKMAXER.—WiIIiam Fletcher, a book- maker, living at No. 5, Vine-street, York-road, Lambeth, London, was on Sunday afternoon found by his wife lying in a place of convenience at the rear of the house. in a pool of blood. An alarm was raised, and medical assistance procured, when Fletcher was pronounced to he dead. There was a deep wound on the threat, and a 143nd-stained penknife lay near. It is believed that Fletcher committed suicide. A BANERLIPT'S PROMISE REDEFMRD.—ME. John fib- bert, corn, flour, and provision merchant, Cardiff, has just done a very praiseworthy act. In 1876 he failed. His creditors accepted a composition of 10s. in the pound, and he promised that if his life were spared and business prospered he would pay them all in full. This promise he has nobly redeemed, each of his old creditor, haring just received a cheque for the balance of his claim. The gift represents a sum of £lO,OOO. PRIZE FIGHT AT MANCur.3tEß.—George Allbinst, a tall, powerfully-built man, was on Monday remanded by the Manchester stipendiary on the charge of coinmittinp, a breach of the peace by engaging in a prize fight on Sun- day. Prisoner and his opponent, for whose arrest a warrant had been issued, fought 14 rounds in the pre- sence of a large crowd. The police suddenly appeared on the scene, and captured the prisoner after a sharp chase. The stakes were £lO a side. Prisoner's face was terribly disfigured. _ _ _

MTSTERICIrS OCCITRANNCIS TN WAT.E9.—A sad death was on Saturday reported from Ebbw Vale, South Wales. It appears that Miss Mary Jones, aged 29, who resided with ' sr parents at Victoria House, lett home with the inten- ,,on of meeting her lover. As she did not return, however, a search was made, and the body was ultimately recovered in Doctor's Pond, near the deceased's house. It is conjectured that in making her way home acros. the fields in the dark, she fell in. the pond and was drowned. The sad affair has caused a great sensation throughout the district, as the family is respectably connected. The police are investigating the matter.

nip EARL OF JERSEY ON PROFECTIOW.—The Earl f Jers, speaking at the annual Druids' festival at Oxford on Monday, said that city had become noted for a resolu- tion passed at the recent Conservative Conference. There were persons present at that meeting who believed free trade was ruining the country, but he differed from tkenr totally. He believed their agricultural friends in seeking-- for pntection were running after a will-o'-the-wisp which they would not secure, and he trusted that that groat industry would not forfeit the sympathy of the people by persisting in such a course. He trusted the improved prospect of trade would put a stop to this agitation.

BEQUESTS AND DONATIONS OF 1887.—The year just closed is described as having been remarkable for the number of large legacies and donations to charities, excluding the many religious and book publishing socie- ties, which the Charity Record regards as trading con- cerns, rith the advantage over ordinary book publishers that they have large gifts of bequests and donations. "The computed figures amount to over £700,000," it says "and adding thereto the innumerable sum; under L'l,ooo, we shall not be far out if we state that the year 1837 should be remembered as one during which at least .€.1,000,000 was credited to the funds of the charities of the country through the generosity of living or departed benefactors."

GREAT FIRE AT A NOTTINGHAM LACR FACTORY.— I E 40,000 DAMAGE.—The large lace factory the property of Messrs. Sharman and Tillson, lace curtain manufac- turers, Newdegaterstreet, Nottingham, was completely destroyed by fire on Saturday. Flames were discovered shortly before midnight, and the fire, spreading with slarming rapidity, soon envelimed the building, wreck- ing the valuable lace and hosiery machinery, and threat- ening the contiguous property and factories. Great alum prevailed. people hurriedly removing their furni- ture and escaping from their dwellings in their night- dresses. The gable end of the factory fell with a tre- menrlous crash upon three cot tages..which the occupants had only a few minutes before quitted. The building was occupied by several sub-tenants. The damage is estimated at £40,000. A SWEETMEAT LOTTERY.—IIEAVY FINE.-011 Satur- day, the Nottingham borough magistrates held a special session to hear a charge against Annie Mont of illegally keeping a lottery in Market-street, Notting- ham. on December 13th. The charge was laid under the 420 d George 111. Defendant sold in her shop packets of sweets, some of which contained coins varying in value from a halfpenny to half-a-crown. A wholesale confectioner in the neighbourhood complained that his business was injured by the illegitimate method of trad- ing adopted by defendant. It was stated that defen- dant had been convicted at a Metropolitan Police court of a similar offence, but, in that case, it was explained, an appeal was now pending. Evidence having been given, it was submitted in defence that it had not been proved that there were any lottery, cards, bills, numbers, or figures used. The magistrates, however, convicted defendant as "a rogue and vagabond," and fined her £lO. FOUR 'PERSONS BURNT To DEATH WHILE Dauttx.—New Zealand papers to hand give the following account cf a horrible tragedy :—A man named Sutton and his wife had, it seems, been drinking at a shanty kept by William Rutherford. They returned to their hut late in the even- ing somewhat the worse for liquor, taking some whisky with them. They were accompanied by a young man named Dougald Mitchell, a brother of Mrs. Sutton, and when he left them, about eleven o'clock, they were going to bed. Later in the night two men. Elliot and Ure, came along. They also had been drinking, and the probability is that when they got to Sutton's hut they had more drink. At about four o'clock next morning the hut was" discovered to be on fire by a labourer named Fitzsimmons, who lived in a tent close by. The hut was on fire from end to end, and the roof had fallen in. The bodies were found in the ruins soon afterwards, and from the posi- tions in which they lay it would seem that Mrs. Sutton and fire had succumbed without making any attempt to escape. Sutton and Elliott, on the other hand, seem to have made some attempt to get out, as their bodies were discovered lyinc together on the doorstep. The bodies were all fearfully burnt, and-presented a horrible spec-' tnele.

A REMARKAIME Minx—John Mansfield Mayville is the name of the inost remarkable boy of the year. Acconii inf. to the Wakefield (Mass.) correspondent of the Net*. l'oek World, he is ten days old, and weighs only iflb. When ho was born he-weighed only Soz. The skeleton is perfectly shaped, and a more symmetrical child never was born. The head is well-lbrmed. and the skin over, the tiny Roman nose laps over the•bone to a point almost as sharp as a knife-blade. Where the frontal and parietal bones join there is a marked protuberance, and, although this is usually noticeable in infants, in this par- k Ocular case it is particularly marked. The lower ex- tremities have all their bones as perfect as in any child. but there is only skin upon them. The eyp of this in- fant is no larger than a pea; every rib can be seen as plainly as though no cuticle covered it at all; the lack of flesh is noticeable on the logs and arms, where:the joints, being larger, show out in contrast with where the smaller and rounder bones are covered with a thick , layer of flesh. The little body is so frail and puny that, it must be bathed in oil, and' this gives the scanty cover- , ing of hair upon the scalp a glossy appearance. John Mansfield, nevertheless, is doing well, and has a marvel- i lona appetite. He is the tenth child of his parents, and bas several very big brothers.

Canon DODD has published in a con- temporary what purports to be a review of the Church of England in 1887; but those who read it will find there is very little in the way of record ,nif the year's work, and a groat deal of what is avouaecUy a defence of the Church on the question of a. t,:blishment and disendowment. With dis- establishmeni in Wales as a part of the Liberal paagn.tmme, it (.:,aes not require any great fore- sight to perceive thai the attack on the State connection in this country' will follow; and we do sur not, of course, profess to Ne prised to find Canon DODD ready to defend the Church of Eng- land "as by law established." We are able to agree with him in saying that the greatest ignor- ance prevails on the question; and we trust his reverence will forgive us when we express the opinion that he himself is in nowise diferent from, erdinar: naert,ala fitintilng in need of enlightenment. Reference is made, in the course of the article, to the special fund of £lOO,OOO, which was set on foot Some teli years ago for the support of the Liberation Society; and then, by way of showing how much superior the Church is as compared with Dissent, Canon DODD proceeds to speak of the millions that have been raised for Church buildings, &c°, during the Past ton years. But surely he must be aware of the fallacy which underlies the comparison; and, if he is, what are we to think of his fairness as a Controversialist? If, however, he is himself 'de- luded when he thus deludes, we are bound to say that gross ignorance of elementary facts prevails to such an extent as to utterly disqualify him for dealing with the question. Suppose we were to pile up the millions that Dissenters, during the last ten years, have expended in building and ' maintaining places of worship, and then put the total side by side with the sum—beggarly by con- trast—which has been subscribed for Church De- fence purposes. Would Canon DODD, would anybody, think it a fair way of bringing the two together " a means of showing what they, severally, were doing as religious bodies? Put in this way, the• question carries its answer with it. If the I'ererend writer wishes to test the power of voluntaryism among Dissenters, he must look beyond the Liberation Society, over whiah he has awkwardly stumbled in this instance, at the thres- hold of his inquiry. Dealing with Church endowments, Canon DODD observes--" It cannot be said that they are in any sense phatever public or national property:' This is a bold statement, but it is 'made, we grant, by an officer of the Church who ought to know some- thing about the matter. Still, there are higher authorities than Canon DODD. Amongst others there is Lord PALIEBILSTON, who said :—" The pro- perty of the Church belongs to the State and the Legislature has the power and the right to deal With that property according to the circumstances of the -times." But why wrangle about a point Which was practically settled by the disestablish- /neat and disendowment of the Irish Church in 1871 ? Did Parliament, or did it not, deal with Church endowments as public and as national pro- Party ? Canon DODD knows, and he ought to have said something about the matter. He might have told his readers, for instance, that not only was the Irish Church disestablished and disendowed, but that, out of the Irish Church surplus, Parlia- ment in the ordinary exercise of its undoubted rights has since granted one million for intermediate education in Ireland, and on million three hun- dred thousand as a Pension Fund for Teachers in Irish National Schools. Now if this could be done with the comparatively poor revenues of the Irish Church, what blessings could be showerecron the People out of the surplus revenues of the wealthy English Church! It is not too much to say that the surplus might be made the means of securing Free Education to the people of England, without taking a single penny from the State beyond the Present grants to our elementary schools. Let the Poorer class of Churchpeople ask themselves if they would not be all the better for being able to send their children to school without the risk of being brought before the magistrates for failing to Provide a school fee when the money was wanted for the barest necessaries of life? Let Roman Catholics, too, take thought on the matter. They know well enough that if strict justice were done —if all Church endowments were applied as "the Pious ancestor" intended they should be applied —there are not a few canons now connected with the Church of England who would either be say- ing mass in the Church of Rome, or going about bewailing that they had not got work to do. We _ cannot, however, have "poetic justice" by giving Catholic priests their own again; but we can at- tain to substantial justice by so making use of some of these ancient endowments that every child in the land, irrespective of creed, shall be Weaponed for the world's fight by receiving Free Education. Turning to another feature of the question, Canon DODD remarks with reference to. the possi- ble removal of Bishops from the House of Lords, that "it does not seem the height of wisdom to banish learning and piety from the Second Cham- ber, and to admit, as not infrequently happens, hare-brained folly and profligate ignorance on purely . hereditary grounds." The phrase, "hare-brained folly and profligate ignorance," as applied to cer- taM members of the House of Lords, is what even critical old PoLoraus would pronounce " good " , and it does seem as if a sprinkling of bishops Would be an improvement. But history, alas! has a sad tale to tell of the influence of such specimens of "Piety and learning" as have found their way

into the Second Chamber. The bishops in• the House of Lords have, not to put too fine a point upon it, been a bad lot. When it was sought to abolish capital punishment for stealing from shops property of the value of five shillings, seven bishops voted against the measuie, and not one in its favour! A large majority of bishops voted against nationalisinff seduotion ; against the repeal of ab- surd disahiliAies:impoked on Jews, Roman Catho- lics, and Dissenters ; against any reasonable settle- ment of the j3urials question ; and it is the bishops, and the bishops alone, who to-day stand in the way of marriage with a deceased wife's sister. In- deed, it is not too much to say that in all great questions which have hail for their objects the im- provement and enfranchisement of the people of this country, the bishops Intsve, as a rule, gone into the wrong lobby. It would mend matte a little, but only a little, "to seleut a certaig number of learned and pious ministers from the Nonconform- ing bodes, and to enrol them in the House of Peers." The true remedy will strike deeper; it will reform the House of Lords altogether; but meantime it can be in some degree improved by doing that which Canon DODD dreads—depriving bishops of their seats under a bill to effect a separa- tion between Church and State.

A number of persons 'were brought before the Newton magistrates, on Saturday last, for allowing their dogs to be at large; and one or two points were raised of considerable interest to those who may be said to love their dogs as wellas their neighbours. Mr. MOISTER, of the Liverpool Farm Reformatory School, Newton, was sum- moned for permitting three dogs to run about in a field some three hundred yards from his house. There could be no question from the statement of the police constable as to the animals being very much at large; but it was urged that, as they were not on the highway, it could not be said that the law was being broken. Two of the magis- trates admitted that they themselves allowed their dogs to go about unmuzzled in their own grounds, upon which Superintendent WEIR said this was contrary to the orders of the county authorities. One of the magistrates—Mr. HOUGHTON—observed that the order was abominable; and the result was that this and a similar case were distrassed. There is evidently a conflict of opinion, if not of authority; and it. wouia 4ét tt) .1M aeslrable to ascertain whether the magistrates are breaking the law when they allow their dogs to go about Inunuzzled in their ow.a grounds. Perhaps Supt. WEIR will bring the matter to an issue by sum- moning one of the justices before his brother jus- tices. Magistrates are never tired of telling re- pentant and unrepentant sinners that their duty is to administer the law—not to alter it or twist it to suit their purposes, It is not to be supposed that they would have any hesitation as to obeying the order of the county authorities—once assured as to the strict legal interpretation of the order. In another case, the defendant pleaded that "the dog's neck was thicker than its head, and the muzzle and collar kept slipping off." The Bench showed themselves not unmindful of the difficulty of dealing with such a dog, and the penalty did not, therefore, ex- ceed one shilling, including costs. The owner of the animal, determined not to be brought up again, made the best of what he considered to be a

bad bargain, by selling the thick-necked creature. In several other cases costs were added to the shilling fine. Superintendent WEIR has his hands full in carrying out the Rabies Act; and the pub- lic will pardon him if he shows himself more con- cerned for humak beings than for dogs. It is evi- dent that the Newton district is well supplied with specimens of the canine quadruped. One may quote Goldsmith and say— _ _
And in that town a dog was found, As many dogs there be, Both mongrel, puppy, whelp, and hound, And curs of low degree.

The discussion which took place at tho meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, on the effects of the beer supplied at the Christmas dinner is anything but edifying. Let Mr. JOLLEY and other guardians minimise the matter as they will, it is on record that the beer had a disastrous effect on the discipline of the Workhouse. The men in an hour or so after the dinner were "singing and shouting as in a public- house," while some of the women made their way out of the Workhouse and came back quite tipsy. More than that, one woman was sent to gaol for being drunk and disorderly; and it is a fair ques- tion to ask whether there was any likelihood of such a thing happening, if the resolution had not been adopted to supply beer along with the Christmas dinner. Mr. JOLLEY seems to have been in a gen- erous mood when he instructed the Workhouse Master (who was beginning with a gill) to let the inmates have a pint each. But he was more gen- erous than discreet; he ought to have foreseen that a pint of beer would have a serious effect upon some people not in the habit of taking intoxicating liquors.. It might also have been foreseen that some would get more than a pint, from the fact that the more abstemious would fail to consume their allowance. As to what consti- tutes drunkenness, there are, of course, very many opinions., Mr. JOLLEY seems to think a person is not to be regarded as drunk until he is helpleSs ; but a Scotchman on being appealed to on the sub- ject went a little further—he contended that a man was not drunk so long as he conld lie on the floor. But without being over-nice as to a defini- tion, we feel bound to say that it is a disgrace to the majority of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians to supply beer in such quantities as to con- vert the Workhouse into a public house under the noisiest conditions, while the women—stimulated by the drink—BO demean themselves as to neces- sitate a letter from the Matron to the Chief Con- stable. We do not suppose any of the ratepayers begrudge the cost of the "pints apiece;" nor is it a question of sentiment in connection with the celebration of the birth of Christ; it is a question of a responsible body of men giving a treat in such a way that it shall not bring discredit upon them- selves and upon the ratepayers, whose represen- tatives they are. It is to be hoped that the evil which has been done will result in the beer supply being abolished. If that course be taken, we ven- ture to predict that the inmates of the Workhouse will be able to enjoy themselves without emulating the worst features of a public house, or requiring the attention of the. Chief Constable.

"The chairman of the Kerry Quarter Sessions was presented with a pair of white gloves at Tra- lee on Monday, there being no criminal case for trial." Tories and Liberal Unionists, please note; Kerry is in Ireland.

The Lymm man who took a short cut across the frozen darn, and f9und that, flopping in, he had to wade Part of the way, has resolved henceforth to "cut short cuts." He believes that round- about is the nearest, after all; and when he men- tions the darn uow it is with a special emphasis.

Edwin Arnold., the scholar, and editor of the "Daily Telegraph" has been knighted--or should we say benighted? At any rate he can now pre- face his name with "Sir "—like Sir Gilbert Green- all, or Sir AB. Walker, or any other "common brewer." How flattering to the author of "The Light of Asia!"

Liberals have got so used to either winning seats or reducing a Tory majority, that they are quite disappointed to and that for once the Tories have a pull. At Winch Otter the Tories have somewhat improved their position, thanks to special local influence. But what of that? Thew must be all exception to prove the rule.

A Commission of the National Football Associa- tion has been inquiring into a charge of profes- sionalism against the Bootle (Association) Club; but no definite decision has been arrived at. As one member remarked—" Best let it alone; for they odo 1." It is with them as with the ladies of Venice, in Othello's time.— Their best conscience is not to leave undone, Bat keep unknown.

It may be said of the Pope's Jubilee, as Artemus Ward said of Shakspeare's grave—"its a success." He is not taking the presents as belonging to him- self—he is dealing with them, shall we say, like an emperor ?or like a man? As for the," preserved meats, fruits, fish, sago, macaroni, tapioca, dates, plums, figs, oils, wines," &c„ itc., that are pouring in upon him, ho is passing them on to the poor, which tio one can say is a poor way of disposing of them.

Speaking at Oxford, on Monday night, the Earl of Jersey said he believed their agricultural friends, in seeking for Protection, were running after a will o' the wisp, which they would not secure; and he trusted that that great industry would not for- feit the sympathy of people by their persisting in such a oourse. But, of course, the Fair Traders will keep "pegging away" all the same; they think they are making i.mgress when they are merely making a noise.

It trauspired that Sullivan't agent had perpetrated a grim joke upon the authorities; he obtained the hall on the under- standing that it was to be used for an iissatilt-at- arms. And Who shall say that boxing is not an assault at arms? _

There was quite a discussion at the St. Helens Town Council about the town clock; it is alto- gether too "slow" for such a go-a-head place. It reminds one of the man who, although he had three hands, never got anything done properly. He had a right hand, a left hand, and a little behindhand. They are about to try to make the clock keep proper time. If that cannot be done, they had better stopit ; for in that case it will i be right at least twice n twenty-four hours.

The Chief Constable of Leeds has directed that in future his men shall be shod with what is known as the "silent" boot, and has given an order for between 400 and 500 pairs. "Oh what a surprise" it will be to "the enterprising burglar," when Robertus drops on him without warning: it will be something like what Byrov calls "silent thunder." The phrase occurs in "bon Juan" : I've but one simile—and that's a blunder— For wordless woman, which is silent thunder.

The Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority find it necessary to keep their eyes wide open in view ti the "Ship Canalers." Huts are being erected in the neighbourhood of Weston; and it was remarked at the meeting of the Authority, on Tuesday, that within a very short time therm would be 700 men at work'at Weston Marsh. Sanitary science can- not be carried to perfection in temporary villages, but in the interest alike of new and old residents, it is the duty of the Authority to do the best they can to secure healthy conditions of existence.

The Duke of Edinburgh has surprised and ills- appointed the governors of the County Hospital, at Canterbury, by withdrawing a five-guinea sub- scription, on his ceasing to reside in Kent. His Royal Highness has long been known as close- fisted. It is stated that the Prince and Princess of Wales were on one occasion buying some jewel- ivy for presents when a pencil case in the form of a screw attracted the Prince's eye. He called the attention of the Princess to the "screw," and sug- gested, so the story runs, that it would "do for Edinburgh."

Mr. Thomas Dyson, solicitor, of Prescot, may, consider himself fortunate in being convicted of drunkenness only, when he frightened two gir' • by pressing his brandy bottle on them in a rail- way carriage the other night—so frightened one of them that she jumped out of the carriage. His solicitor admitted that he was in "a morbid drun- ken state," which was most likely true, though we do not see why he should have added that it was "not singular at Christmas time." Mr. Dyson has escaped with a fine of 30s. and costs; but he has a lesson which ought to sober him for the rest of his life.

There is considerable discrepancy in the state- ments as to the suitability of South California for emigrants. The climitte is undoubtedly good, and wages are high in some parts—Los Angelos, for instance. But employment is by no means certain, and if a workman gets double wage, and is out of work half his time his position is by no means im- proved. If the place were a Paradise to begin with, it would soon be so overrun as to become an average bit of earth. The law of compensation holds good there and everywhere. Workmen can- not be too careful in making inquiries before emi- grating. Fortunately, there is plenty of informa- tion to be had if they will take the trouble to hunt it up and compare notes.

The Rev. L. Price has been emptying the vials of his wrath upon the head of the Mayor of Lowestoft for daring, on recovering from a serious illness, to announce that he would give a public ball. "A cursed ball," the reverend gentleman calls it, and he adds—" You never heard of Moses or the Prophets, or Christ or his Apostles, giving a ball." Of course not; but is the inference con- clusive? There was a certain old lady who went to remonstrate with a new " meemster " for preaching in a gown; and she appealed to St. Paul. "Who ever heard of St. Paul preallhing in a gown ?" "Just so," said the " meenister," "but who ever heard of him preaching in breeks ? " The old lady was silent, if not convinced. How would it be to put it in this way to the Rev. L. Price?

The Wirral Highway Board seem 0 be pushing things hard against Mr. T. A. Walker, the con- tractor for the Ship Canal works. They have de- manded E• 200 for repair of roads through the extra traffic consequent upon the work which is going on within the jurisdiction of the Board. The extra traffic, it should be stated, has been going on for a month only. Mr. Walker, through his agent, suggested that the roads should be main- tained for twelve months, and he would then pay the difference above the average cost; but this reasonable suggestion has,))een set aside, and in- structions Oven to take, proceedings for the recovery of the amount claimed, if not paid within a week. The members of the Wirral Board are not very considerate; they do not deserve to benefit by the Canal.
Our neutral contemporary publishes what pro- fesses to be a "London Letter." One paragraph

In the last "Letter" begins :--" When the news Of the proposed bounty on the exports of cattle and meat from the Argentbie Republic first reached our shores last autumn we gave publicity to the .tale. Its official confirmation in the cfr- respondence which we publish to-day between Mr. Stephens and the Board of Trade, will anew attract attention to the subject." Is not the use Of the editorial "we" suggestive ? How could the correspondent, if in London know of the , "correspondence which we publish London, know Can it be that, figuratively, he writes in London while in reality he writes in Sankey-street? Such things have happened when newspaper proprietors have come to show more n.tgard for economy than for accuracy.

ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.-011 Thursday morning Mrs. Porter, wife of John Porter, grocer, &c., West-street, was walking across the shop when she fell into the cellar, through the trap-door which she had previously left open. FIRE AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORKS.—About te minutes to five on Tuesday evening a fire broke out on the "new plant" of the Lancashire Alkali and Sulphur Company, Ditton-road. An alarm was immediately sounded by the steam whistle, and within a brief space of time a number of policemen, with a hose, and the Fire Brigade, under Superintendent Carr, .were on the scene. Fortunately, the workmen had previously succeeded in extinguishing the flames with brine, a quantity of which was stored in a tank In A :cinity. The fire originated in a small shed upon the top of a tower, and the damage is very trifling. A gas jet is lupposed to have been the cause of the outbreak. The ' duties of secretary were well felf "led by Mr. P. Quinn, and tlyre of La asu-er by Mr. Mulch. Mr. Match also ofFeiated as M.C. SINGULAR DISAPPEARANCE OF WATCHES FROM A TRAIN. A young man named Thomas Prescott, in the employ of "ka Mr. Pownall, a watchmaker, St. Helens and Widnes, placed seventeen watches and a pendant in a workbox, on Wednesday, and proceeded from the last--named town to St. Helens by the 12-19 train. The watches had all been left to be cleaned, and Prescott placed the box on the rrck, and entered into conversation with two work- ingmen who Were in the same compartment. The train ran into St. Heleas at 12-41, as usual, aat the rear of a tmAn from Liverpool to Carlisle and the NeLh, and Wid- res passengers going in that al rection had just time to enang,e. Prescott says he got out of the carriage and left the box on the rack, but remembered it as soon as he got to the ticket gate. He ran back to the compai.,- ment but the box was gone, and his fellow-travellers were nowhere to be seen. The train was searched by the railway officials, but no trace of the box or its con- tents, or the men could be found. Information of the suppered robbery Wa3 reported to the railway and police • authorities, who instituted inquiries. On Thursday ' morning, two men named Mark hallantine, labourer,' . 58, Derby-street, St. Helens, and Thomas ,Carey, fire- man, 76, Atherten-street, entered'Mr. Pownall's shop and placed the box containing the property on the coun- ter. They stated that they saw the box in the carriage. and that they had a parcel of bread and cheese on the rack near to it. On leaving the carriage they took the box by mistake. They took it home and opened it, avid having found that the watches were Pownall's they had brought them to him. Prescott says he did net see any parcel on the rack belonging to the men. Thu men were given into Custody. Loss OF A LOCY%-TRADISOG SCHOONER. Thursday night. at ten o clock,•the erevv of four men belonging to the schooner Margaret, of Dundalk, from Garston to Dundalk with coal, put into Port St. Mary in a small boat after 33 hours without food. The schooner foundered 25 miles W.N.W.. of of the Chicken d Lighthonie in a gale of wind. The crew were nine hours at the pump. They left her at rifle o'clock on Thursday morning. No lives were lost. The crew were in a very exhausted con- dition. The vessel was uninsured. The loss is esti- mated at .8850. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT KNOWSLEY HAIL.—At eight o'clock on Friday mot ming the household of Kno sley, the seat of the Earl of Derby, was thrown into consternatien, as the groom of the chambers, llohn Devar, aged twenty-nine, was discovered in one of the rooms under his charge with his throat cut in a dreadful manner by a razor. lie was dressed ready for his usual duties, bust he appears to have premeditated the rash act by the preparations he had made,' the door-of the room having to be forced open. Dr. R. Gorst, medical adviser to Lord Derby, was immediately summoned, but so serions was the injury inflicted that it was thought advisable to call in also Dr. Henry Gerst, Huyton, and, after% consultation, the injured an was removed to the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool, where he now lies inw very critical condition. No motive can be assigned for the rash act.

Addresses were given by Messrs. Garnett (chairman), R, Cook, and C. E. Par- ker, and Mrs. Parker. Mrs. Garnett had the manage- ment of the tea and concert. Mr. P. itowden pre- sided at the pianoforte.--At a later hour the Wesleyans of Penketh. according to their usual cus- tom, held their watchnight service in the school- room, when the Rev. G. E. Young, Warrington, preached an excellent sermon from the 60th Psalm, 12th verse. There was a large congregation present. After singing the well-known hymn, "Came let us anew our journey pursue," and pronouncing the Benediction, the meeting closed.

BRUTAL ASSAULT AT WV:INES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. H. Wade Dea- con, a young man named Joseph Kelly was brought up on remand charged with un'awfely wounding Joseph Mills', lodging house keeper, Oxfo-d-stieet. The evi- dence of several witnesses showed that on the 26th December the prisoner, who was accompanied by a wo- roan, applied at Mill's house for lodgings. Mrs. Mill declined to receive them as inmates. At ails time the prosecuto- appeared on the reene, and the p:isone: im- mediately attacked him with great violence. He knocked the prosecutor to the ground with his fist and whilst tie was prostrate kicked him several times, indicting serious 'wounds. Over the right eve was a contused lacerated wound, an inch and a half in length, penetrating to the bone.and there were alsoseveral cuts. The prosecutor had esides two teeth knocked out and several others loosened. The injured man was in danger for some days.but under the care of Dr. O'Keeffe he was now progressing favourably. - -rhe prisoner. who made no reply to the charge, was committed to the County Quarter Sessions for trial. RUNCORN BOARD Oe GUARDIANS.—The .Jli meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Worb'muse on Tuesday. There were present Colonel Ashton (chair- man), Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood, Messrs. Mclntyre, Taylor, Aaron, Grice, Stokes, Lewis, W.Whit- low, Hadfield, Brandreth, Hewitt, Smith, J. Whitlow, Turner, and Pickering: H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—The Rev. J. Lockwood, in reading the report of the relief supervision committee, stated that the collector was getting on with his work in an admirable manner and to theeatisfaction of the coin- mitee. £l2 124 had been paid as commission for the work already done, and, of course, the morethey had to pay for commission, the better it was for the Guardians and the ratepayers of the Union. The cases had been brought before them in a business-like and orderly man- ner.—Mr. Hadfield read the report of the Finance Com- mittee, which stated that the deputy-clerk had made an application for an increase of salary. Thedeputy clerk's salary, Mr. Hadfield mentioned, was £lO a year, and in consideration of that payment he did the law business of the Guardians without costs.—lt was decided that the application be referred to the Finance Committee, which was supplemented by the addition of a number of Guar- dians.—Mr. Hadfield also gave notice that he would at the next meeting move a resolution in accordance with the proposal that the Finance Committee might make.— The Workhouse Master reported that two pigs had been destroyed owing to their having had swine fever.—ln the course of some discussion as to the prevalence of swine fever, Mr. W. Wnitlow alred if the veterinary sur- geon was paid his fee when a case turned out not to be one of swine fever.—A Member : No.—Mr. W. Whitlow: Then they w;ll all be swine fever. (Laughter.)—The Workhouse Master also reported that a number of pre- sents had been sent to the mma tea, and a vote of thanks was returned to the donors.—The relief cases were then proceeded with. VIE TALK OF TRE TOWN.—BOWEarI Golden Kerb Pills.— RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTRORITY.-TllO fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. There were present Colonel Ashton (chair- man), thellev. J. Lockwood. Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron. Hadfield, W. Whitlow, Stokes, Brundrett, Lewis, J. Whit- low, Smith, Turner ; H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector.)—A letter was read from the Local Government Board with refer- ence to canal boats. It stated that the total number of boats snspeeted whilst passing through the district of the Sanitary Authority during the past vearwas HID, and the amount of remuneration paid to the inspector was £lO per annum. No legal proceedings had been taken dur- ing; the year, and no cases of infectious disease had come under notice.—Mr. Mclntyre. said he considered the re- pot tto be a satisfactory one.—Mr. Farrington reported that in accordance with the instructions of the Authority he had written to the Ship Canal Company and also to Mr. Walker, the contractor, stating that in the event of any building being erected for human habitation in con- nection with the Ship Canal in the Authority's district such habitation must be provided with a sufficient supply of wholesome water within reasonable distance; and in the event of any similar building being erected in the townships of Frodsham and Frodshain Lordship it was imperative that plans be submitted to the Authority foupproyal. He (Mr. Farrington) added that as yet no reply had been received to this communication.—Mr. W. Whitlow asked if sanitary arrangements would not have to be supplied to the buildings erected in connection with the canal as he was told that it was intended to erect them in villages.—The Deputy Clerk said if there was any nuisance caused it would here to be removed.—Mr. W. Whitlow said that action had been taken by the Altrincham Union.— The Deputy Clerk said that in Altrincham Union they had urban powers, but in the Authority's district they had not these powers except in Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship.—Mr. Aaron said he understood that before long there would be 700 men em- ployed on Weston marsh.—Mr. Farrington said it was a matter of importance to the Authority that works like that of the Ship Canal were generally followed by lerry builders who ran up a dozen houses in about a fortnight, and into which they let people go before any proper pro- vision was made for them. He understood that an applica- tion had already been made to a landowner for land to build houses of this kind upon, but it had been re- fused.—Some discussion took place as to the advisability of applying for urban powers, but the subject was dropped without any action being decided upon.—This was all the business of public interest. NAVAL APPommENT.--Captain Jones-Parry, who appears in this week's " Gazette " is promoted to Rear Admiral on the retired list. He joined the Royal Navy in November, 1845, and had been in active service until last November, when he resigned the appointment in the Clyde, to reside with his brother-in-law at Thelwall Hall. Several years of this long period of active service were spent on the lEast and West Coasts of Africa in suppressing the slave trade. lie was gunning officer on board H.M.S. Terrible (then the most powerful and heaviest armed steamship afloat) in the Black Sea during the whole period of the Crimean war, six years instructor on board H.M.S. Cambridge (gun- ning training ship), and finally nearly fifteen years superintendent of the CUmberland in the Clyde, on leaving which appointment he was presented by the ditectors with a handsome piece of silver plate. 'RUNCORN MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. The annual tea party in connection with the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Mission to Seamen, was held in the Mission-room, Bottom Locks. The weather was very unpropitious, but notwithstand- ing about 150 persons sat down to tea. The tables were presided over by Mrs. Mettdowcroft, Mrs. Rirkham, Mrs. Bell, Mrs. Wiswall, Miss Statham, Mrs. Abil, Mrs Reed, and Miss Taylor. Subsequently hn entertainment was given, under the presidency of the vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, and the room, which had been very appropriately decorated by the Sunday School teachers, was crowded. _ _ . _

The pmceedinis commenced by the Rev. T. Patrick, M. k., of Liverpool, charkiin to the missions, delivering a brief speech, in which he dwelt upon the efficacy of prayer, and the necessity' for the observance of the Sunday as God's Day. During an interval later in the evenincz,

Ths Vicar delivered a speech in which he said that any work for the benefit of sailors must be interesting to Englishmen, for such a great deal depended upon. our sa,lors. If we had not plenty of sailors how should we carry on our manufactures, and get our bread and butler? (Roar, hear). Sailors led a hard life on board ship, and seldmn heard anything for their spiritual good; whilst on shore, at home, and abroad, they were sub- beet to many temptations. It was therefore good that there were such hAtitutions as the Mersey Missions to lead them right. He was told that Runcorn was the metropolis ef barges: and he was sure that everybody ought to give their best support to the work Mr. Shaw was doing amongst boat people and their children, and amongst sailors. '(Applause). Assistance was rendered to the Church by such missions, and it Wig desirable that all people should feel that they had an absolute right to go ta the Parish Church. (Applause). The Vicar then referred to the size and position of the present mission room and suggested that a larger and more conspidious building on the other side of the locks would be of greater advan- tage to the sailors and boat population, as he Was told that for one sailor that passed the present mission- room ten passed along Percival's-lane. (Applanse.) Mr. Shaw was the most successful beggar in Runcorn— (laughter)—and if the townspeople would only kelp him, they might before long see a more commodious room pro- vided for the mission in Runcorn. (Applause). Mr. Meadowcroft, hon. secretary to the missions pro- posed a hearty vote of thanks to the ladies who had pre- sided at the tables; and also to those ladies and gentle- men who had entertained them by music and recita- tions. . .
Mr. Allen seconded the proposition, which was carried unanimously. _ . _

Ms. Wiliiam Shaw, the missionary, then proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies who had provided the " fruit" on the Christmas tree ; and otherwise helped them in their Christmas festivity. He said that ladies and gentlemen had last year made particular inquiries concerning what had been done amongst the boat people and sailors, and one name he must mention was that of Lady Broke, Norton Priory. (Applause.) That lady made great inquiries about the mission room, about the boat people, and about the workand the accommodation which was provided for them in Runcorn. He explained how rnali the room was, where it was situated, and its awkward position. (Applause.) Now, there was one question that might be asked=" Where were the sailors that night ?" They might ask the question very often. Last Sunday night week, if he had been asked, he could have said "Here's one." and he was very thankful to see him. He expressed the pleasure he felt at seeing the sailor, who said he NVZIA pleased to be there; but that he had been trying for an hour to find the mission-room. There were some people who had come to the town for years and yet could not find it. He believed that where there WM one sailor who came near that room there were thousands who passed along Percival's-lane. He was very pleased with a remark Lady Brooke made, when she asked whether he did not think a reading-room should be provided for sailors, where they could smoke their pipes and read the papers. He replied by saving that that was just what was pro- :ded for in other ports, and that that was what was wanted. He was pleased to hear Lady Brooke say that if it was intended to go in for anew mission-room he must let her know, and she would do what she could towards the subscnptiods. (Applause.) He hoped that by that time next year they would have a new mission-

room twice the size of the present one, and one which ' sailors could find without searching the town for an hour. If they had a mission-room in a more suitable. place he guaranteed they Would seethe sailors attending it. (Applause.) A ship's captain, who was in the room, said owing tra, its situation the present missioa-room was dangerous ttr get at. If it was situated in another part of the town there would be a good congregation. Mr. Ilulme seconded Mr. Shaw's proposition, which was carried unanimously. The entertainment was of an enjoyable character. A.trio, consisting of Miss Jones and Messrs. R. Morris and J. Birkett, gave two selections with 'good effect; and songs by Miss Taylor, Miss A. Randles, Mr. J. Pownall, Mr. R. Morris, and Mr. L. Crosby were highly appreciated. Recitations were given by Miss Bertha Holland and Mr. Millington; whilst the Misses Crosby • skilfully performed a pianoforte duet, Mr. F. Mack a piccolo solo, and Mr. H. Grounds a pianoforte solo. Miss E. Crosby ably officiated as accompanist.

PROPOSED BUILDING OPERATIONS : A SEWER QUESTION.

The minutes of the Highway and Building Committee contained a recommendation that a cheque be drawn on the treasurer for the sum of £3 3s 9d, such sum to be re- turned to the owners of property who contributed to the sewerage repaireat the back of Shaw-street. It was also recommended that 500 handbills, referring to the written notice required by the building bye-laws, to be given to the surveyor by a builder, of his intention to cover up ary sewer or drain, be printed and circulated. The plans ot Messrs. J. and .W. Farrell, junr., for the erection of 14 cottages and one shop in Salisbury-street, and of Mr. Henry White for the ereation of 12 cottages in Chaucer-street, and eight cottages :a Salisbury-street were approved.—Mr. Speakman moved, and Mr. Han- kinson seconded • the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Meadowcroft, alluding to the refundlng of the money to the Shaw-street property owners, contended that the Board was not liable for this expenditure in remedying - anu - nce, and quoted from the Public Health Act in suppdrt of his view.—Mr. Lightbum sald a case similar to that under discussion had been decided and the town i was responsible for the expense.—r , Law Clerk said he had quoted the cases to the committee, but he had not the referenca with him that morning.—Mr. Meadowcroft still argued that the drain was a pr:vate one, and ulti- mately the recommendation was referred back to the comm.:ft on the motion of Mr. Meadowcroft.—Mr, Lightburn, who seconded the motion, said he should be glad to find that the Board was rot responsible for the back passages. It would be a serious matter if the Board was responsible.

div.head: ANAL BOATS ACV:.
div.p: ANAL BOATS ACV:.

The annual reporL as to the execution of the Canal Boats Acts had been prepared by the sec •ctary. and it was approved, and ordered to be forwarded to the Local Governmeat Board. During the year, the report stated, 13 boarts had been registered, making a total of 859 boats registered at Runcorn &nee the passing of the principal Act. Seventeen cases of infringements of the Acts had been dealt with. There had not been a case of infectious disease reported in the district during the year. The salary of the Inspector was £2O a year.

FINANCE.-11AD VENTILATION. The Finance Committee reported that during the past month the receipts amounted to £789 17s 6d, and ac- counts amounting to £321 4s were passed for payment. It was recommended that the teneer of Mrs. Elizabeth Meadowcroft, executrix of the late Wm. Meadowcroft, for the loan of £l,OOO. for a tcrm of five years, rate of interest 31 per cent, per annum, payable half-yearly, be ac:tepted, and that the Law Clerk be instructed to pre- pare the nece4sary bond. It was also recommended that the tender of Messrs. Thomas Kirkham and Co., for the painting and papering required to be done in the reading room, book stores, offices of secrel sry and inspector of nuisances, kc., for the sum of £lO 9s 6d, be accepted. (Other tenders—G. Yarwood, £l3 15s: W. (lrayson, £l4 8s; A. Tonks, £18.) It was resolved that the fol- lowing assessments be reduced :—H. Handley, Bridge- street, £l2 15s to £8 lOs ; H. Jukes, Irwell-lane, £l2 15s to £l2; S. H. Kirkham' Hi3h-s., £26 5s to £22 15s. Mr. Imison moved the adoption of the minutes, and ob- served that the public had confidence in the credit of the Board was seen in the fact that they were able to borrow money at a quarter per cent, less than they advettised for.—Mr. Speakman seconded the me :or, and suggested ' that Messrs. Kirkham should not commence their work until some efficient system of ventilating the various rooms in the building had been carried out. At present there was no ventilation whatever, and it was a very serious matter to those who had to sit in the heated and foul air.—Mr. Lake said it was thtte the committee dealt with the ventilation.—lt was understood that Mr; Speakman's suggestion Would be acted upon, and the minutes were passed.

div.head: ItEmcir., OFFICER AND THE HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE ItEmcir., OFFICER AND THE HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The Health Committee recommended several persons for registration as the keepers of common lodging houses. —Mr. Lightbarn moved, and Mr. Pritchard seconded. the adoption.—Mr. Imison asked whether the whole of the minutes of the Health Committee were recorded on the agenda.—Mr. Lightburn : So far as affects the Board they are.—Mr. Imison claimed to have the minutes read, and after some persistency succeeded.—The Secre- tary read as follows :

It was resolved that the following extract from the nuisance inspectoe's report be sent to the medical officer : "I beg to report that I have made an inspection of cot- tages in Back Mersey-street. and, found 19 cottages empty. Some of them have not been occupied for some and are in a most filthy and Vapida.ted condition. These cottages before they are fit for habitation will re- quire cleansing, lime-washing, and airir The Inspec- tor, in reply to the committee, stated that he had made. the inspection at the request of the medical officer of health. It was resolved that the med. -al officer of health be asked to state in writing his reason for asking for the above report. It was also resolved that in future the medical officer of health address any reports on the sani- tary or unsanitary condit:on of any portion of the town to the committee in the first instance.—Mr. Imison said that was a resolution that ought not to stand on the books of the Board, as it would seriously prejudice the medical officer in the discharge of his duty. He was not sup- nosed to give reasons for his instructions to the nuisance.- inspector, and were he to do so he might lay himself opezo to an action. As to the menical officer reporting to the • committee instead of the Board. M. Imison condemned' that resolution as unwise, and charged the. Health Corn-- mitten with supineness, and with having almost ignored the doctor's reports on several occasions.—Mr. Light- - 'burn. as chairman of the Health Committee, replied that the inspector had examined the houses, and had found nothing objectionable to public health in them, and so the committee thought it was only reasonable to ask the medical officer to what he objected in the premises. FIP denied that the committee had ignored the doctor's reports, and said the present method of submitting them was like talking to the gallery. He contended that accordle to the rules of the Board the report should be made to the Health Committee, and he pointed out the advantages of such a course.—Mr Lake said the medical officer was justified in his action by, the report of the nuisance inspect& wha said the propferty was in a filthy and dl'apidated condition. The medical officer of health would not have done his duty had he • not made the suggestion he did, and to address such a resolution to a prAfessional man and a servant of the Board was unfair.—The Chairman ruled that the discussion should not continue on a matter that was under the consideration of the committee.—The Secre- tary said he had strict instructions from the chairman not to put Upon the agenda any matter that as under consideration. and that was the reason the minutes under discussion did not appear.-Ultimately the minutes. • were passed.

Mr. Hankinson wished to know if the Waterloo Bridge Committee were doing anything.. The bridge was in a very bad state indoed, and the committee had been in existence for a very low; time.—Mr. Pritchard said the committee were not in a position to say.anvthing until they heard from the Law Clerk.—The Law -Clerk, said he was waiting to bear from the Canal Compa,ny.—Mr. Lightburn said the bridrre was in a beastly condition.—Mr. Speakman de- scribed the disgraceful'condition of the bridge, and sug- gested that Mr. Barker should make a footnath three feet wide. If the committee did not quickly make a commencement with the improvement of the bridge the cost would be increased by ten per mt.

Statistics show that Nottingham, when compared with other provincial cities, is fully as sanitary and healthy; indeed, there is no reason why this should not be so, for the pure water, fine surroundings, and untainted air all combine to make this most satis- factory state of affairs. During the past season, however, there has been an alarming increase of certain kinds of diseases, and while the dryness of the season, and consequent exposure of impure matter, have doubtless contributed to bring this about, there is, as yet, reason to believe an increase of mortality, the result of natural causes, is taking place in our midst. This fact is especially true with reference to those diseases which affect the kidneys .and liver. An alarming increase of complaints which arise from the derangement of these func- tions furnishes an adequate reason for investigat- ing the matter, and in order to thoroughly do so a representative of Messrs. H. H. Warner and Co. has made some careful inquiries, and with the following results:-- An alarming increase in a short time in diseases of liver and kidneys was found to have taken place e and when these troubles are not promptly and properly met, they result in other troubles, and the most serious con- sequences ensue. Many persons were found who Had suffered, but by quick action and the use of proper medicines had been able to escape any serious conse- quences. The representative found that in most cases a widely-advertised remedy was the medicine used, and in each instance the result had been most satisfactory and beneficial, and with these facts before him he started on a tour of inspection among those who sell and those who use this wonderful remedy. The first call was on Mr. Jesse Boot, manager of Boot's Pure Drug Company, at 18 and 20, Goosegate, who was asked what he knew of the use of Warner's SAFE Cure in Nottingham. Mr. Boot replied that the sale of this remedy was exceedingly large' not only in Nottingham, but in both their branches in Sheffield and in Lincoln— in-fact, for the space of time it had been before the pub- lic the demand was the largest he had ever known ; and that this large and constantly increasii g? demand con- clusively proved that Warner's SAFE Cure possessed the merit claimed for it. Mr. Cook, the chemist of Hyson Green, also spoke in high term.e of the SAFE remedies, saying that thedema,ml for them was large, and that he was doing a very brisk trade with them, and that they were evidently giving the greatest satisfaction on all sides. Mr. Hopkins, of 88 and 90, Alfred-street, South Not- tingham, was the next chemist visited by the reporter. Mr. Hopkins spoke in the highest terms of praise of the SAFE Remedies, especially the SAFE Cure, and said that he had personal knowledge of several instances where the greatest benefits obtained by patients were from its

use. . The next chemist met was Mr. Allsop, of 39, Dennian- street, New Radford, Nottingham, who said that he was being constantly asked for Warner's SAFE Cure, and that in one case in particular of severe liver trouble the "Cure" had proved most effective. After listening to the chemists, the representative next sought out some of the persons who had been personally benefited by the use of Warner's SAFE Remedies. The • first subject was Mr. William Deaken, of 7, Tudor Grove, who stated that the remedies, in his opinion, had ac- tually saved the life of his wife. She was so weak that she could not walk uPstairs or lift a book from the table, all resulting from severe liver troubles, constipa- tion, nervousness, lee, As a last resort, and after the doctors had said they "could do nothing for her," he had tried Warner's SAFE Cure. Four bottles had resulted in wonderful recuperation, and that continued use had en- tirely cured her of all troubles except the nervousness,. which was entirely mastered with Warner's SAFE Ner- vise. Mr. Deaken said he could honestly and confidently recommend the SAFE Remedies to the millions who were suffering, and that he was always ready and willing to give his experience to anyone, for he felt so grateful for the good they had done his wife. • Mrs. Mary Maltby, of 22, Connaught-street, Radford, Nottingham, stated that for eight or ten years she was a great sufferer from nervous exhaustion combined with constipation aad severe pains in the ;Jack, and every few minutes would have to sit down to get relief. She had tried doctor after doctor, and had gained no relief. Finally, she secured some of Warner's SAFE Cure, and from its use had obtained the greatest possible benefit, and had the greatest faith in its merits. Mrs. Ellen Yeomans, of 42, Garden Street, Radford, stated that indigestion had made her life miserable for two years, that she could seldom take a meal, was in- ' capacitated for her ordinary household duties. She had tried all kinds of remediae and many doctors, but with- out any good resulting, until Mr. Shippam, the chemist of 120-, Denman Street, told her husband to try Warner's SAFE Cure. The result of the use of this medicine was marvellous, and she had been enabled to resume all her duties without any trouble. Mr. Wm. Keyworth, of 78, Moffatt Street, Notting- ham, was very emphatic in his endorsement of Warner's Sars Cure, and said that its efficacy could not be doub- ted after a fair trial. It had cured him completely of nervous debility and dizziness in the ‘head. He stated that he always kept it on hand, and would not be with- out it. The conclusions which the people of Nottingham must inevitably draw from the above reliable facts are these: first, that the increase of these serious complaints of the kidneys and liver is such as to cause careful concern; and secondly; that a pure and certain remedy has been found which will prevent the approach of these eliseastes, or, where they have become seated, will furnish a cure. div.head: PADGATE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS.
div.p: PADGATE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS.

The fourth annual prize distribution in connection with these schools took place at the Institution, in the presence of a number of visitors, on Tuesday. The Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Sutton) pre- sided, and he was accompanied on the platform by Mess-s. W. Derbyshire, J. Greening, and J. Bonnell (members of the Board of Guardians), the Rev. S. Wilkinson, (Chaplain of the Schools), the Rev. W. H. Williams (vicar of Padgate), Mr. Mines ~(superintendent), and Mr. Naylor (assistant school- master). There were also present, amongst others, Mrs. Mines (matron), Dr. Peacocke (medical officer), Messrs. John Houghton, William Houghton, R. Kilshall (Guardians), Mrs. Ward (matron of the War- rington Union Workhouse), Miss McEvoy (school- mistress at the Padgate Schools), Mr. Samuel Sut- ton, Mr. and Mrs. Fairhurst (industrial trainer and portress), Mrs. J. Houghton, the Misses Bennett, Mr. Henry Thornton, Miss Thornton, Mr. Thomas Houghton, Mr. Joseph Houghton, sen., Mrs. Wood, Mrs. Barrows, Miss Fairlie, Miss Whittier, Mr. Joseph Houghton, jun., Miss Watkins, Mis-t ,Scott, Mr. lutes, and the Misses Melt. The room was tastefully decorated, and a Christmas tree that was placed at one end of it had hung to its branches a number of toys, for the children. It had been pre- pared by Miss McEvoy and Mr. Naylor.7-4ddressing those present, Mr. MINES (superintendent) explained' the principle on which the prizes had been awarded. The best worker in the "Horn.," to which he or she be- longed. the best knitter, the best tailor boy, or Shoe- mar.er boy; the boy, With great integrity of purpose, Or willingness of purpose received prizes—merits of this kind were ,of more Importance than were educationall attainments, and prises were given for everything they thought would promote good conduct amongst the chil- dren of the schools. He had, on behalf of the Children of the schools, to thank the numerous subscribers for their kindness. The sum of £2O Is. 9d. bad been col- lected, and they had spent £l7 153. 6d. The 'amount subecribol this year was larger than it had been hitherto, and the prizes were of a better character.-After distributing the prizes the Mayor, in the course of a few remarks, said that it was highly important that the children should be wellisclucated, as without education they could not expect to attain to any .important .posi- don in society. The Guardians and officers, of. the ;in- stitution did ail they possibly could to improve their minds, and the children ought to take advantage of the opportunities which were now presented to thern,remem- bering that when they left that institution the same facilities for acquiring information weruld not be exten- ded to them. C;otne of the greatest men who had ever lived had received their educations in institutions similar to their own, and that fact alone should serve .as 'an incentive to them to do all they could to make themselves well informed. —On the ,motion of Mr. GREBNINS, seconded. by Mr. NILBY91111?.E, his Worship was accorded a hearty vote ef thanks for his services.—The Rev. W. H. Williams hav-i ing addressed a few words of encouragement ' 'to the ! children, the Rev. S. WlLKlNSON,speaking -as chaplain of the Union, said that the children received a good prac- tical education based on religion and if they made use of it they would.be able to succeed in life.—An interest- ing musical programitie was then gone through. An orchestral band under the leadership of Mr. Peter Cald- well, jun.l played several pieces during the evening-; songs were given by Miss Colbourne, Miss Bonnell; Miss Williams, Mr. Mercer, Mr. Booth. and Mr. lkin ; and violin solos were given by Miss Parry, and a duet, flute and violin, by Messrs. Walsh and Brimelovr. Miss Sud- low and Mr. George Riley were the accompanists. The National Anthem was sung at the' close of the pro- ceedings.

div.head: LOVE AND LEARNING,
div.p: LOVE AND LEARNING,

A well-known, elderly nobleman; of large. wealth, wooed and won, a few years ago, a young and very bea.utiful girl._ Their life has been as happy as it is pis; sibka for married life te be, when December is Milted to May. Hi S lordship is distinguished in scientific circled and and possesSes high literary attainments. Sometime after hi,imarriage he was foolish enough to think that his lovely , wife waS not sufficiently educated, and laid out a course of reading for her. A month later be inquired alsint. her progress, , and found that she had not opened a book. Reset up his.eye- brows after the maaner of old husl?ands when their young wives have displeased them. Whereupon she looked up at bins with a bewitching smile, and said: I was .made to be loved, not to be learned. She wort the day, of course. 'What is learning compared to the light of a sunny blue eye? Would not a busbara rather be met with a 4mule and a kiss, than by a wife who assured himthat she' keew her lesson ?" Wisdom La all very well, but winning .wave go further. Laughing eyes beat Greek roots all to nothing. A woman's lovely tresses, waving on the outside of her shapely head, are more precious in a husband's eyes . than ever so much 4earning io- side cif it. Therefore, all women should endeavourto preserve their attractions. and welcome their liege lamb with loving looks. pleasant smiles, and flossing silken tresses, for after all a boautiful head of hair is the clowning charm of a woman, a charm which all , may .possess by using Hrs. S. A. Allen's , World's Hair Restorer, which will keep the hair healthy and strong, restore gray or. faded hair ;to its original color, and Make it soft, silky, wavy and luxuriant. It may be had of any chemist or perfumer.. •

pack on the line Warren relieved by a grand run to the quarter flag, but the aplendid kicking of the Yorkshire backs again forded the game. over the line, a dead ball resulting. Soon' after a drop out the whistle was blown for half time, the score being—Trinity one try and two minorsto one minor. The home team re-started, 'and play settled at centre. Pretty passing by the visiting team was lewdly applauded, but Ash came to the rescue of his side with a huge punt to the Warrington quarter flag, Nevins returning. The home team rallied, but Dairies 'got in a good kick, Only to eise Latham struggling to cross the line. Warrington saved, but the drop out still found the game in the Warrington territory. War- ren, Speakman, Barnes, and Jolley indulged in some neat passing, taking the play to halfway, and a good run by Barnes was replied to with a neat dribble, in which Lathatn, Harrison, and Booth were prominent. 'Talley put in some strong work, and ft screw kick by Speakman forced the game into neutral ground. Harrison almost got-hi-for thelonee-team, and altar- tiOttift preety.,paseing. lye the Trinity becks, Ash aseteyed a drop at goal, the ball going wi,3e. Fotherby replied to the drop-out, the ball going dead. Hamehaw recommenced, and Fair. Turner—who was now playing • forward, 'Rattan taking his place at back--caltered Dawson!, before he could return, and the game rested in the Wakefield 25. .Tolley put in a punt to Hamehaw, and collared the opposing full back before he could make ' headway. The Warrington meg playel with renewed vigour, and a kick by Ash to Nevins was well returned in touch close to the line. Ashton here passed to Fair. Tur- ner, and the latter transferred to• Bandies, but the Trini- tarians wore too quick for him. Barnes got in e huge kick to Hamshaw, but the safetacklingof the Lancashire men prevented his replying. Warren almost got over after a grand run, being brought down on the line, and wild passing lost the advantage gained. Jolley was now to the fore with a strong run, Lowrie safely holding,- him closeto the line. From a pack here Speakman passed to Barnes, but the coveted point was not scored, only a minor accruing. ft was fast becoming dark, and the players were scarcely discernible across the field, but grand efforts were made by each opposing team to add a major point, butwithout avail,and after seventy minutes of an interesting and pleasant game Wakefield Trinity were pronounced victors by one try and seven minors to two minors. The Warrington team are to be congratulated on the show they Made with their powerful opponents, and al- though defeated they were certainly not disgraced. The forwards all worked with limiting energy, and baffled their opponents with smart passing and dribbling. But ,for the powerful kicking of the Trinity backs, the result would assuredly have 'been reversed. Of the backs War- ren took the palm, and, indeed, it was hard lines for him, after the grand run he had made in the second • half, to be brought down just on the point of scoring. Speakman was always on the leather, his saving of the strong rashes of the opposing forwards gaining for him high praise. Jolley had not much work, but what he had was done in finished style. Barnes played fairly well, but the remaining position at three-quarter was weak. Nevins at times showed to great advantage, and compared favourably to his more experienced oppos- ing full back. On behalf of Trinity, Ash was a host in him- self, his kicking being a treat to witness. Able . assistance was rendered by Fotherby;Dawoon, Whiteley, , Lowrie, and Latham. The following were the teams :—Warrington: , Nevins, full back ; Jolley, Barnes (captain), and Fair. Turner, three-quarter backs ; Warren and Speakman, halfbacks; ,Ashton, Frank Turner, W. Dillon, Hayes.'Randles, Povev, , Davies, Littlewood, and Craghan, forwards. Wakefield Trinity : Hamsha,w (captain), full back; Fotherby, Fat- , las, and Apt, three-quarter backs; H. Dawsonencl,Dunn, . halfbacks; Latham,Lowrie, Booth, Harrison; liThitaley, Jones, Thomson, Ross, and J. Dawsoneforwards. Um- pires, Messrs. Gilbert and Parry. Referee, Mr. E. lies- wick, Swinton Football Club.
