Owing to the late arrival of the visitors, it was a quarter to four before a start VIM made, conse- quently a game of 40 minutes only was played, out of which Widnes came victors by a goal, two tries, and three Minors to one minor. Directly after the kick-off 1)7 Smith, Farrell ran to the visitor quarters. and Par- kinson made a fine but futile drop at goal. A dead ball resulted. Widnes continued to press, and then the home quarters were invaded. Parkinson 'relieved grandly by a run and kick. Plumpton followed with a dashing run to Failsworth quarter, where he named to J. Bingham, who dribbled over the line and Plumpton secured a try. Kiddie failed at the place. Fine play by the home for- wards having compelled Failsworth to save; half-time was called, with the score—Widnes one try and two minors to nil. Immediately after the kick off Widnes ' had hard lines for scoring, a minor being registered. A few minutes later the ball travelled into the home terri- tory, and a visitor tried to drop a goal, but only secured a minor point. A splendid piece of play now ensued. Parkinson passed to Farrell at Failsworth 25. That player ran to the line, and then passed grandly to Hughes, who obtained& trybahindtheposts, from which Farrell landed a neat goal. Subsequently Hughes after a fine run obtained another try near the touch flag, S. Bingham failing at place, and the game dosed as above stated. Teams -.-.Widnes:: S. Bingham, back; Plump- ton, Parkinson, and Farrell, three-quarter-backs ; Wil- kinson and Pennington, half-backs; Smith (captain), Hughes, Kiddie, J. Bingham Gandy; Barber, Woods, H. BLUNDELLSA•NDS IST.— These teams met on the Wilderspool Causeway ground on Saturday to play their first fixture. The visitors wore strongly represented. whilst the home team were very much weakened owing to injuries and sickness among their men. A good number of spectators assembled to witness the contest, and the home captain kicked off at 3-30 from the Wildorspool end, Eyes making a short dribble, the ball going into touch in the visiton; quart ters. Adamson broke away from the line-out, but was stopped by Freeman. Whittle passed to Evans, who kicked well, but Alty replied with a strong run, being brought down by Sanson. Thornley- next broke away and drilbled to Clarke, who put in a long kick, and Sanson missing the ball, Jolley kicked into touch in centre. A good effort of the visitors was neutralised by Warburton kicking into touch. Wright next passed to Freeman; who put in a strong run, hut he was safely brought down by Sanson. Evans transferred play into the visitors' quarters by a grand kick into touch. Biwa- dellsands worked the ball out of danger, but Antrobus got hold from a line-out and put in a good run, but passed wide to Warburton, and Alty. dribbled Ito centre; Evans saving. Antrobus next made his mark, and some good kicking between Freeman, Warburton' Clarke, and Jolley took place, the ball going into touch in mid-field. Wright got possession from a scrimmage and kicked to Jolley, this player, putting in a tremendous punt, and Adamson and Eyes following up almost scored, Norris saving near the line. Shortly after the drop out An- trobus got away and passed to Stinson' this player putting in a high kick, and, following up, lie and Antro- bus took the ball over the line, the latter player succeed- lng in grounding the oval. Jolley failed at goal. Both- well re-started, play resting in the visitors' quarters. Thornley was next conspicuous with a dribble, and Alty replied with a short run and kick into touch. Evans put in a high kick, and following up secured the ball and passed to Eyes, this player and Whittle taking operations to the visitorS' goal line. Blunciellsands gradually worked the ballot° centre, when the librne team, headed by Uns- worth, Neill, Eyes, and Whittle, took the ball over the line, it dead ball resulting. Clarke dropped' out, tho ball going into touch, and, from the lino-out, Adamson secured and Passed to Antrobus, who put in a splendid run, being brought down by Clarke. Evans now re- ceived a pass from Whittle, and made a very good at- tempt at goal, another minor being registered for the home team. After the drop-out the visiting forwards dribbled, to the home territory, but their stay was of shore duration, as from a scrimmagp Adamson and Donohue broke away with a dribble, the former player picking up nicely, but missed a good chance of scoring throwing forward. The Blundellsands' forwards removed play to the Warrington half, when Sanson got hold and kicked, but the ball glided off his foot, and the home team had to save by kicking dead. On thd half time be- ing called the scord stood—Warrington 1 try and 3 minors to Blundallsands 2 minors. Bothwell re-started for the visitors,Evans returning nicely to centre. Antrobus secured possession and put in a short run and kick, Freeman responding with a strong run, being pushed into touch bY Holland. Alty got in a good kick, and Jolley being held before he could part with the ball, play rested in the Warrington 25. The home forwards worked the ball to centre, and Antrobus obtained a free kick, Jolley almost landing a goal from the place back. Whittle next passed across the scrimmage to Antrobus, who went off with a Strong run, the full back checking his career, Whittle kicking into touch. Atty intercepted a pass intended for Evans, and macle.tracks for the home lino, Jolley stopping his progress. From a line out in the 'visitors' 25, Whittle made a dribble, Adamson crossing the line, but lost possession of the ball; a minor point accruing. Evans returned the drop-out, Freeman returning into touch. Whittle passed to Sanson. who ran the ball to the line, Blundellsands saving by kicking dead, .The home team scored another minor from a kick by Sanson, and on call of time the score stood—Warrington 1 try and 7 minor points to Blundellsands 2 minor points Teams :—Warrington Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Stinson, Evans, and Warburton half backs, Whit- tle, and Antrobus; fortvards, Donohue, Adamson, Eyes, Thornloy, linsworth, Bate, Neill, Holland, and Holmes. . _ The Warrington team journeyed to Wakefield on Sat- urday to play off their.first annual fixture with the 're- nowned Yorkshire cup'-holders. It has never boon . the good fortune of the " wirepullers " yet to lower the colours of the Yorkshire men, but although they have been defeated they have, nevertheless, given their oppo- needs -a good game.' = On Saturday some doubt existed as to Whether the match would take place, owing to the severe frost that had prevailed during the past few days but a rapid thaw having set in On Friday, no difficulty was found in bringing off the match. A first-elass saloon having been planed at the disposal of the team,: through the kindness of the London and North-Western Railway Company. a pleasant and comfortable journey was made,, Wakefield being ' reached at 1-20.. The -ad- vertised time to, kick off-2.45--only saw a moderate at- tendance of spectators, the result of a rumour that no . match would be-played, owing to the death of, the presi- dent of the Yorkshire Rugby Union. Each team failed . to Muster its full strength, but Warrington was at the greatest disadvantage', being minus Massey and Rigby, ' and it is a hard task to find one to fill the place of the first-named player with anything like confidence. Hut- chinson WEi3 away from the .ranks of the Trinitarians; but an able substitute 'was found in Dunn: = Barnes' having lose the toss, Frank Turner commencOki opkationC from mid-field, Ash returning well at =centre ! flag. After some exchange kicking by the 'opposing back% Speakman "made his, mark," .but Falla.s tiega- tired the advantage gained by a smart run back to mid- , field. Fair Turner tried to get away, but was well tack- ! led, and from the ,scrimmage formed Latham gut away, and made a grand run to the Warrington lines.' Jolley relieved the preAmre, and Dunn was awarded "a free kick, but Barnes was to the fore by m huge return kick to Midfield.. From some loose play Dawson pa.s:3ecl to Harashaw, the latter punting to the Warrington quar • ter-flag. Lowrie headed a dribble, Speakman saving in marvellous fashion. , The Warrington forwards, headed by Ashton and W. Dillon, now took play to neutral ground, but.the splendid kicking of Ash and Fotherby again forced the visitors back, and Ash, who was awar, ded a free kick for a fair catch, scored the, ,first: minor for' the home team. Bandies shone with a neat run soon after the. drop out, and as the result Of. some pretty passing by the Warrington backs the , game rested in Trinity territory... The Warrington team now held the upper. hand, and pressed the Yorkshire men back on their lines. Warren next gave IlarneS chance, that player dropping at goal but failed, a minor resulting. ' Idarnshaw dropped out, and, after some give- and-take play, the visitors were found again to be in.the ascendency, and, -a neat run by Jolley was appauded. Barnes now looked dangerous; but Fallas relieved by a. timely kick to midfield. Dawson here passed to Ash, who transferred to Fotherby,. the latter kicking across the lines; and Nevins mulling the ball, the home for. .wards were quickly in attendance, and Ross was enabled to score the only tangible point of the game. 'Whiteley ' essayed the kick at goal, but failed. Soon after the drop out, Fotherby almost got in, Speakman stopping him. The home team now assumed the aggressive, but from a • • ei

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

WarringtoU certainly ,met toemen "worthy of their steel," as the saying goes, when they- encountered Wake- field Trinity on their own ground on Saturday., Nobody who hali any regard for probabilities expected that they would be able to overturn the grainier Yorkshire team. and speculation was mainly rife as to the balance of points that Might be notched against them. The result of the game, therefore, was by no means 'a disappoint- ment to the admirers of the local team, but rather the • contrary. If the Trinitarians could only manage to gain an advantage of a try and a few minors on their own ground, we may perhaps fairly anticipate that their efforts will be altogether neutralised evertif not eclipsed when they come to Warrington next Saturday. Warrington spectators will to-day.have an opportunity of seeing new faces and perhaps new styles of play when the Rugly team turn out to meet Barnes contin- gent. A tight and high-class game may be expected. Runcorn should have • journeyed to Manchester on Saturday, to play the return match with Broughton Rangers, but in consequence of the hard state of the ground the fixture was abandoned, and the wearers of the Green lost the opportunity .of wiping out their de- feat of three weeks ago, a task they felt confident of accomplishing. On Monday, despite an -unpleasant downpour of rain, and the sloppy condition of the field in Irwell-lane, a game between "past and present" was brought off. The spectators were far from numerous, but those who did brave the storm were rewarded by an hours' amu.sement,Thorne ludierous incidents occurring. Of course the past had to retire Ignothinously defeated. To-day Oldham visit Runcorn' and a grand game is anticipated. The hicks will be at a disadvantage as, several second team men are being tried, and "Billy" Riley is to partner the Captain in thp responsible position of half-back. It is to be hoped he will prove worthy of his trust. Victory" is still the cry of the Widnesians. who are. beginning to wish for mightier foes. On Saturday Fails- worth had to retire well beaten, but although they only managed to score one minor point, the game was a really, fine exhibition, and the visitors were frequently danger- ous. Of the home team, Kiddie, and Parkinson played in grand style. Morris and Hardman were absentees, • and sterling players as they ate, it is rumoured that they are not likely to again don the jersey for the chemicals. No doubt capable substitutes can be 'found.

THE SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A PRESCOT SOLICITOR., ' The Prescot Police Court -wascrowded on Tuesday, when the charges against Mr. Thomas -Dyson, .solicitor, • Prescot, amain came on for hearing. A keen interest in the proceedings was manifested, and the case seemed to,. form one of the principal topics of conversation through- out the district. There were three 'cliarge:s against the prisoner, viz., that of being drunk in a rail Way carriage; of assaulting Rose Coulter, and fUrther Of annoying and interfering with the comfort of passengers'. Mr. Dyson, wilt) was represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift (St. • Helens), pleaded guilty to the charge of • drunkenness, and not guilty to the other two charges. Mr. Preston, jun., of Liverpool, appeared on behalf of the London and Xerth-Western Railway Co., and said he did so under somewhat painful circumstances. The des.' fondant, he was sorry to say, was a solicitor practising at Frescot, and besides a charge of assault—which was the principal one—there' were minor charges of ititerfer-t. jug with the comfort of passengers and of being drunk. He narrated the circumstances of the ca,sa, and asked the Bench to deal with the defendant as he.deserVed• He was a man in a inost respectable position, and ought to have known better. • ; Ada Shannon said she was a domestic servant for Mr. Isaac Fountain, of Elm. Cottage, Huyton.":.. She was ,for-, merly in Myrtle-street Orphanage, Liverppol,- and she , was new 17 years of . age. On the'night of the date. named she and Rose Coulter left Li*erpool for, Htlyton. "by the 11-10 p.m. train. . They were placed.' in the Car- riage by one of the Orphanage teachers. It was a third , class compartment, and witness sat with her baekto the i engine and her companion on the other side: •• At 'Edge ' Hill the prisoner got into the train. - Just after thetrain i• had left Broadgreen, witness remarked to her con pueiou that it was well they did not miss the train. The &fens dant then spoke to her; and she said she' had been to a' party. He asked, "Is that true F" and then offered them a bottle of spirits. She and her Companion reftised to take any, and the defendant after this got upfto shut the window; but the witness; said she would rattier have , it open. The defendant sat: down near the companion of witness, and in doing So removed a parcel .that was between them. The then, stood up, and the 'defendant hold • out one of his arms behind her. Witness was frightened and screamed, and immediately afteiivards jumped from the 'carriago,Mr. Preston ' What were you frightened at ?—Mr. Swift objected to the :question, and said it was a question of two hysteiiAtal girls taking , fright.—Mr. Preston: They were frightened:at something: -Mr. S wif t liutyou must only saywhat the defendant did. —Witness, continuing, said she was frightened at him offering the whisky and sliding along the seat. She ne-kt ! remembered rolling' down the embankment, and after that she went th a . house where she was directed to • Broadgreen. In reply to Mr. Swift witness said .she had to climb over 4 wall after she jumped fromthe carriage She told a man whom she met on the road to her home that she had missed her train,: and ,she asked him if he could get her a car. The defendant did not atternpt to ' do anything to her except to ask her to have. a drink. She did not know that the -defendant, was drink; he looked sleepy. She knew she had not reached Huvton wiain she jumped but. - • ' • .Rose Coulter said she was also a domestic servant at ' Elm Cottage, Huyton. She.gave evidence hi corrobora7 ton of last witness's statement, adding that after her companiOn jumped out of the carriage she tried to fol,low her when the defendant caught hold of her and heldlier Up. She remained in thispoSition until the• guard came • and•got her into the carriages I .t - -John Brierley, the guard ipf, the train, stalKid that 4.fter the train left Broadgreen station lie hoard screams, and on putting MS head out of the, windew he saw one of the , girls jump out of the train. Tie -stepped on to the foots board; lila walked to the compartment.. Where the door was opdri. Ho got to the carriage 'with a great deal of trouble,' and tried to pacify- the.girhandget her inside,. She said she would not ride with the defeeclant any fur- ther. He said he would ride with -them.. Witness was afraid she was going to , jump on him, and knock theni both off the step. She was so frightened. he eould get nothing out of her. When he got the girl jute the, cars riage, he said to the defendant, "What is the meaning of this ?." He replied, "Mind your oWn business ; I know what I'm doing." Witness: travelled with the 'del fendant to Roby, where the train wastitept for eleven or twelve Minutes. He sent a party telook.fer.the girl that had jumped out of the carriage. He got some 'other gens tlemen to. go into the carriage With the 'defendant while he Went to knock 'up the stationmaster:-s-Creassexaml 'hied The train was going at the rate, of tivdnty' to twenty-five 'miles an hour when the girl • jumped' out... When he got to the carriage Dyson was sitting quite still. He was drunk.—Mr. Swift: I suppose you bring out plenty of drunken people by that train? Witness ; • Very seldom. Mr. Thomas Lloyd, stationmaster at Roby; deposed that the defendant, after being asked three or four times; gave his name as Dyson, of Prescot, but he shortly. afterwards said that was wrong. Tha defendant after- wards stated—" On approaching Broaclgreen Station the girl got up, opened the door, and deliberately jumped out. I put out my arm to prevent her. There were several others in the compartment who took no notice whatever. On arriving .at the' next Station I gai,o
OUR LONDON LETTER.

, LONDON. InunsoA.v NIGHT. - As far as human judgment goes,: the New Year opens with every prospect of. prosperous times. The At cloud which lurked round Christmas time , has been uplifted, and everyone has,eoriie to the con- ' elusion that Peace is, at least for the present, as- sured, a condition of things which goes some way towards eecuring the desired end. We may pos- sibly have the war scve again in the spring,:a much more reasonable time for its prevalence, and that is the only drawback to. the roseate view Of things taken in the commercial world to-day. Even as it is, the irrefragable record of the Stock Ex- change shows how much better off we are to-day than we were twelve months ago. In. almost all stocks dealt in, advance has, been made, in some ' cases, copper for example, a Very substantial ad-. vance. Cooper is now More than twice the price it was last New Year's Day, and the copper mines have moved up pewi passe., With respect to railway stock there is a general and substantial advance in all stocks, except the hapless Metropolitan, and, in. much less degree, the South Eastern. Higher lances for railway stock meansincreased business from the vastest manufac- tory to the smallest shop, and.if the prophets. are right we are only at the beginning of something like a boom in railway shares. Moreover the prosperity attending upon Great Britain is reflected on-vaster scale in Australia and America. In the United States the revival of trade has been apparent for many months, and is now unquestionably established. i;.A.ustralasia has been suffering through its length and breadth with a succession of droughts which checked its prosperity. According to latest advices plentiful rains have fallen, and the prospect is brighter than it has been, for many years. I suppose we must not grudge Lord Salisbury's' Government the substantial advantage they will reap from this harvest, which 'certainly -they have not sown. They are 'exceedingly hard up for some means of recummending themselVes tg.favourable notice, and they will findit in a considerable surplus. Before Lord Randolph Churchill ttiok his Russian trip, he dealt a little blow at Mr. Goschen, whom he bitterlyhates, by announcing that he would have a surplus of three millions. That he would haven. surplus at all was Mr. Goschen's own secret at the tithe, which he cherisked with the intention- bf making it known in due season. Lord Randolph nOt only robbed him of this pleasure, hut, by over-, stating the probabilities, discounted th e legitimate effect of Mr, Goschen's good fortune. People have come to leek for &surplus of three millions, and if Mr. Goschen has only two at his disposa4there will be growling instead., of congratulation. That is what our genial friend, now in Russia, sought to enjoying the success of brinr.,-, about, and is greatly his little plot.' Still, Mr. Goschen will; withui good luck, not common with, his predecessors in recent times, have a substantial surplus. It is understood that it will be applied towards 'giving a start to the local government scheme; which is. to h'e the backbone of the sessional programme.. This. scheme, if carried out, will be another example of the Cou-, servatives stealing the Liberal thunder. Mr. Glad- stone has always been in favour 'of trlnsfeiring certain imperial. tiaes to the local bodies in aid of local rates, and, the Local Government Dill, which', Mr- Ritchie is to bring in next session, is mainly founded on that. which Sir Charles. Nike drew up, and Mr. Chamberlain adopted With some slight modifications. . Mr. John Morie3r is happily through the Valley of the Sh4dow'of Death lie was:lately walking in,, ' and only no*. wants rest and change of scene to bring him back to. big old form. There is a, report: about that he mews to retire from. political life and go..bAck to his books.. I dare say it is possible he has that hankering, for he is, first of all, and above all, a literary man. But the Liberal party'eannot , do, without John Morley, and the profound sense of , duty that dominates all his actions will ,keep in the forefront of the liattle, certainly, till it is Won. Talking with him just before he left for TO/quay, he spoke with enthusiasm of the pleasure he found in recurring to his books. Ile was then reading "Boswell's Life of Johnson," a handsome copy of which' had just reached, him from Lord . Rosebery as a present on his birthday. I remember Frank Burnand experiencing just such joy in his convalescence when, on returning from Royat last amnion, he passed dangerously near death's door. ,He found time to read over the old books, and his great discovery and delight was "The 'Christmas: Carol." For the busy man the time of sickness has its advantages if there only comes the Jong hours of convalescence when he may go back to his books, ' which in active life are thrust aside by the impor-' tunate newspaper. ' Lord Derby_ , has _been_ keepimg_Christmas at ' Knowsley in the good old-fashioned way. He dines ouea good ddal in London during the season, but Lady Derby has of late been handicapped in her , social relation's by growing Weakness of the eyes. She is, to tell the truth, which she does not in this particular like to admit, even to herself, nearly blind, and goes only to houses with the interior arrangement of which she is so familiar that she . Can walk about without fear of 4isaster. Her lady- ships stubborn imperious way df ignoring decrees ' of Nature which 'do not please her is indicated in a ' little story which some of her dearest lady friends , are fond of retailing. Lady Derby's age is nowhere ; on public record, but the lao friends aforesaid , agree that she is at least two years older than .her

husband, who will not see his sixty-second birth- day till next year. However that be, the question of age is, with a single exception. never Mentioned in Lady Derby's 'presence. When the Chinese Minister first brought his wife over here, there was great anxiety on the part of society to make her a lioness. hut Chinese etiquette did not readily per- mit one of her birth and rank to mix with outer barbarians. Eventually it was arranged that she might, one 'afternoon, call on Lady Derby, upon the understanding that no gentlemen were to be present. Lady Derby invited about' •a. dozen ladies to meet the Minister's wife. They sat in an ex- pectant circle waiting her arrival. She came in due course, curtsied, and was enrtsied to, and then„ planting herself immediately opposite Lady Derby,; said "How old are you ?" This, it was subsequently explained, is the Chinese mode of greeting, much as we say "How do you do?' But the embarra.ssment of Lady Derby, and the consternation of the select circle may be imagined.' Mr. Swinburne used to be seen a good deal about a certain class of literary and rather Bohernian so- ciety, and was a frequenter of two somewhat ex- clusive clubs which keep exceptionally late hours'. Of late, however, he has withdrawn to himself and.„. to the society of his old friend Mr. Watts, whos6 chambers he shares. The principal reason for-this is a growing deafness, whieh has practically shun him off from general conversation. T lis infirmity ha& not improved a temper-always a little irascible and lately inflamed by the- action of his former hero-Mr. Gladstone. There. is a story current of him at one of the clubs alluded to, which trate& his manner. He was talking to an .intimete- friend on some question of the day. Another mem- ber of the club, a somewhat fussy pushing-rams-4- overhearing the drift of the conversation joitted in and laiddown the law inperemptory terms • burne 'with his hands behind his back, his head held down, seemed to be intently listening an atti- tude-which encouraged the-intruder to eialtirge-withs• fuller unction. When be had Quite finished, Swig- • burne looked up at his friend and quietly said "My dear fellow, come over to my chambers, where we can talk without being interrupted," and taking his arm walked him off, leaving the undesirable person for once in his life abashed. , I hear—as a curious illustratiOn, of the badness,of the times—that the number oft "rankers" who have recently enlisted is beyond precedent in peace times. In old days young men of good family would enlist • out of pique, or devilry, or despair. The cases were isolated, but the examples were always fortbcoraing. The same motives, no doubt, operate now. But in more than one instance I am told that candidates who could notpass the examination has e joined the , army the only way left to them, by enlistment. In one of our cavalry regiments there is at this mo- ment a young trooper whose grand uncle was a peer. On the other hand, I hear that ordinary soldiers come from a very much better class-than heretofore. Indeed one can easily see that the military status has improved even though the old stagers assure us that the service is rapidly going to the dogs. . At some of the theatres the managers have hit on the happy expedient of running their old pro- gramme through the early weeks of the holiday season and then changing their bills. Thus they get the same public twice over. For instance, at the Strand Cellier'e "Sultan of Mocha" will be withdrawn in the course of a fortnight, and "Babette," a new opera eomique, substituted In this, too, a part will be found for Mr.. Ernest Birch, who takes the title role in the" Sultan.", Mr. Birch i 5 either son or nephew of one of the governors of the Bank of Ireland, and has the courage to act under his own name. I think Mr. Sugden was the first to adopt this rule. It was, suggested to him not to appear under his family name.. He replied that his family had done nothing to disgrace him, and that till they did he'd keep .his own name. Miss Emily Faithful' writes :—"My attention has been. called to a paragraph in the London Letter last week relating to nay article on Ladies in Business,' quoted in the 'Pall Mall' as 'Lady Shopkeepers,' which probably led, you to Misunder- stand the work done by Miss Charlotte Robinson, as you allude to her as a saleswoman rather than a house decorator, &c. 'This is, however, a matter of no special importance, but as% would seem I had

- led to the mistake I tbought. it would better to enclose you her circular. I am. glad you mentioned the MisseA Garrett, for they have done excellent work also." What was written about Miss Robin- son was a reference to her "enterprising careerat Manchester as a saleswoman of. artistic work and house decoration." If Miss RobinsOn is not a sales- woman, I hope she is a woman who has sales aS she deserves success.

, -WIDNES BAPTIST CHAPEL.—SALE OF WORK. A sale of work was held in this place of worship ? on Monday, with the object of increasing the funds already raised for the purpose of building a new . . chapel. The edifice in which Widnesians of the Baptist persuasion at present assemble-to worship, in addition to being in need of rather extensive repair, is situated in a district that is far from suit- able. At the time the building was erected it was anticipated that Cromwell-street woad be in the centre of the town, but, although the land was laid out with that end in view, trade and commerce took a direction quite unexpected, and the carefully arranged plans of landowners and builders had to •be altered, The Baptiste Chapel is now hidden! in - an obscure back Street, and sh;aost oyershadowed by a • large chemical works, whilst the approaches are far from inviting, The members of the denomination have been greatlhandicapped in their labours by these eireUm- stanom, and for several years they have been unceasing in their ender-ours to accumulate money to enable them to remove to a more central and conveni-e" i out situation. • The sale Of work 'oil :MOrlday was yet 1 another effort, and despite the inclement woather there -1 was a good audience at the opening ceremony. Mr. David Wright, in performing this•duty, made-a ' 1 speech in which he said it. afforded him mush pleasure to I have tha Opportunity of meeting his Baptist friends that , afternoon. No doubt everyone of them.', felt glad that GQ1,1,1 in His meecy,, had spared each. of. their lives - through another year. Looking back.they could think, perhaps, of sdnie persona they knew who Were living with them last year, and to whom life was probably as bright then as it was to those present now. (Hear, hear.) But the only thing they pould do was 'to trnst that they had rested froth / their ' labours, and that their works would, follow. them. (Hear, hear.). It was a grand thing to live, and espetially when at the last it Could be said,of them that they had -done some little good in the world. He was glad to meet with the ppoole of any. section of Cluist's Church who were try- ing to improve their own lives' and at the 'same time improving the condition of theirfe,llow creatures. Non- conformists had sometimes to labor under very great difficulties. It frequently happened that they had no e rich people nonnected with their chapels, and 'often I. when a person amongst them did get rich he left them ei in the search for better society and a, better church. ,He I did not k.,aree with that practice; he liked to cling to the church of his fathers.. (Hear, bear.) ' They could' not all have fine churches in the" best situations, , there-, ' j fore let them try to•dothe best they could under exist-, ..1 Mg circilmstances. (Hear,. hear.). Where there were willinghands, willing.heads, and willing hearts, almost anything could be accomplished, and he was confident that if thee continued tense the perseverance that now disting,uislied them.theY would attain the laudable lob- ject they had in view'., (Hear, hear-.) He. should be proud, to afford them all the help he possibly 'could. (Applause.) In, conclusion he wished those present a happy and prosperous New Year and declared the sale open. The Rev. 11. Yeatmart moved a vote of thanks to' Mr. Wright for the kind service he had rendered that day ; and in doing so remarked that although they .were few., in number, the•llaptists of Widnes lipped and believed that there would, be an improvement in their position by-and4oye. The.inembers of the church and oongrega-: tion had worked very nobly inconneetion with the effor. they were making from year to year to raise a fund for 'a new chapel. They had now nearly ' £3OO deposited in the bank in Liverpool, and this had been raised without, going outside upon any regular system Of begging. They • had been in negotiation for the purchase of a site in Victoria-square, and the matter was practically settled, and the land might be transferred at any time., The, price would be £3OO. He trusted they would soon have raised enough money to Make a definite start With thenew chapel. He earnestly wished to get away from their present situation, because the place neither outside nor • inside was far from prepossessing and inviting, and in fact looked dismal. He wished they could get some of those people who had money to come forward; he thought that. they would' conclude that as far as the reads Were concerned they Wanted a neWchipeL (Ap- plause.) . . . - The ,Req. D. Davies, Welsh Congregational minister, seconded the motion, which wasvarrie'd by acclamation.

Thesale then commenced. Goods of the usual char- acter were displayed on two stalls, presided over by Mrs. Yeatman. and Misses Passey, Woods, Maokereth, Rat- cliffe, and Priestnall. The refreshment stall was in charge of Mrs. Davies, Mrs. Robinson, and Mrs„Calland. stall upon which were artiolee provided by the voung Men was attended to by Messrs. HER GREATEST HAPPLNESS.
Vide ," W waria MAIL," CARDIFF, Saturday, Oct. 15, 1837.. '
11ISS KEW:WM ,of 7, Clive-road, Canon, Cardiff. wa sufforing from a most severe „form a
Ilness. She had the advantage of the very best skill and care, but all appeared vain; and she Wai at last sec:ion-mended to

go to the Waroorgan and Ifoninouth Infirmary, Here ,she was treated for several weeks for Bright's disease. Mlk diet, vapour baths, and other prescriptions had no effect. On the. contrary, she became much worse, and her body commenced

• to swell. Mind, in March, she underwent an operation, and • some 16 or 18 quarts of water were removed from her side and legs. She continued to get worse, and In May was discharged as incurable. Her journey to her. home (then at. Kings- brompton, near Silverton, in Somerseteshire) was performed with the greatest difficulty and suffering, and occupied;arveral days. Though a cure had been pronounced hopeless, her father nsisted on further professional advice, and again inetra- meats were applied, with the frightful result of withdraw- ing 20 quarts of voter from her each week. Again the mediT eal men pronounced the case hopeless, and Emily they re- linquished attendance on that ground. The unfortunate was now in despair. Her sufferings were indescrib- able, and there was no prospect except that et sink lag through slow torture into an early grave. At this time she became acquainted with the detells of an extraordinary cure (the well-known care of William (Irayson) by Hop Bitters, and she resolved to try them. MedScal men sanctioned the experiment, but warned

hec that tt could only be a useless expense. However, Miss Melhuish palliated, and in June she began to take the Bitters. Her conalttlon changed almost immediately. The water diminished, to the surprise of the doctor, who had measured her at intervals, and who declared that the change was noth-

ing short of miraculous. The improvement continued; she gained appetite, and slept well, For months previously she bad been it.d-114° to retAin fo,d, o t filoy Continuous rest. Within two inonths the water was practically checked,. She continue& te use the Hop Bitters, finding that .they,atrength; ened her„ in addition to relieving the disease, and within three months of her commencing to take them she was able to

walk in the fields without help. This astonishing cure of one of the most awful diseases that affect humanity has made the deepest fropreerrion on both professional and lay inhabitante of the dislaiet. Miss Melhubdr, the fortunate subject. of what she regards as almost a miracle, is now able to walk her seven or eight miles with ease. With a proper sense of grateful ap- preciation of the remedy, and with a laudable desire to help ether sufferers by the diffusion of the precious information, she anuouncoastSuut her greatest happiness will be to show her fellow eveseures who may be suffering the tortures of this hideous dlrlpase how they may find relief. "Dear Fred,—You will be surprised at receiving a letter from me, but, thank Clod. I am pleased to say I am getting better every day. I shall be so giad• to breathe the fresh air again. It has seemed a dreadful long tine to be in bed. You know I was taken to the hospital last April to be treated for Bright's Disease of the kidneys. Well, on July 31 they tapped me, and took away 304 «moos of water. The same thing was done again on September 18, and 408 canoes of waterl obtained. On Oct. 9 I was dholsered from the hos- pits& as Ineumble. In January this year (the 20th) was again tapped at home, and 360 ounces of water taken aWaff. The St. Bartholomew's Hospital in London refaced me admission as a hopeless case, and the St.. . Bartholomew's Hospital, Chatham, also refused me, as being the worst case they had seen for years, and two local doctors gave me up as hopeless. When I camel from the hospital it book three to put me to bed. My clothes had to be cut off. I was an object of misery and despair. After the hospitals had refused me, and doctors given me up, my wife persuaded me to try HOP BITTERS, and from the commencement have Improved daily. I have only taken them seven weeks, and can now get downstairs and walk about without even a stick. With the aid of a few more bottles of the Bitters hall be well again. The water has left my body and' legs. The only trace left is in my feet. It is a wonderful medicine. I wish I had tried it sooner, as I have nearly • ruined myself and family with doctors bills anditther expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the hospital I had no appetite whatever, but since using the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The only difficulty is the expense, but must not mind that so long as lam getting walL Am cheerful now that recovery Is near, for evei7 one had given me up as a bad job.—With best wishes
" Your affectionate brother,

'BOARD OF OIT'ARDIA.NS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held ' at the Workhouse on Wednesday m.,rning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. J. Greening, Isherwood, Derbyshire, Jolley, Blackh'urat, Ctflrke, Rgtêliffe, W. HOughtrin, J. ' Houghton, Wright, Bonuell, Balharry, Gralige, bert, Owen; J. C. Sutton (clerk),S.Sutton,(assistant ' clerk), Ward (workhouse master). . • ABLE,BODIEO MUTES. On the House Committee's minutes corning up for con- firmation,.Mr. Isnanwoon said there were one or two able-bodied inmates of the house—about 39 year Of age —whom they could not get shot of. They Were always either there or in gaol, and the (iimrnittee would like to know if they could turn these persons out.—The CLIME said there was no doubt. that they had the discretion to turn anyone out of the Workhouse, but they yvOuld have to consider what vconl4 become of hint, and if he Came back the next day on an ()icier of the relieving officer they would be no better off:' He would suggest that if they had a man in the Workhouse who was able to work, they should give . him plenty- of work to do, and if he disobeyed the orders, send him before the magistrates, and the probability would be that he would have tO.go to, ISHERW a OOD men- tioned that they had young fellow Miskell in the Worknouse. He was known to assault all the" new policemen that cameinto the town, and he hakrcome straight from gaol to the Workhotise.—Mr. Ginnonno, who occupied the chair in the early part of the meeting, said the only Nyay to deal with people of this sort was to give them plenty of work. As for MUM, he had been often before the magistrates.—The WORIEHOLTSE MASTMR said that on the 25th December Miskell went out on the plea that he was going to chapel, but he did not turn up again till after five o'clock. Last Sunday he forced his way out of the Workhonse, saying that he would go in spite of the master.—Mrrlsrisawoori : Ilewas one Of the ringleaders on Christmas Day in asking for more beer.-L Mr. GREENING said that when anything of the kind that had been mentioned occurred the proper course for the master to take was to send for the pollee—Mr. JOLLEY suggested that the master should. be instructed .to send for the police when any insubordination took place, and have the refractory inmate locked up. This was neces- sary for the good management of the house.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE remarked that Miskell should be informed by the Board that he must not go out again, but a gug- ges.tion of the CLERK that Miskell should appear before the House Committee was agreed to.

_ PADOATE INDII;THIAL SCHOOLS. The School Committee recommended that as the heat- ing apparatus of the Padgate Schools was ineffective, the present boiler be taken out, and a larger one substituted by the firm of Messrs. Greening and Sons Limited.— After a short discussion the minutes were passed, on the motion of Mr. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. IsnaawooP. THIS cnalSrmas DINNER.—INMATFS "ON TRH LOoSE."—

ALLEGED EVIL EFFECTS OF THE HEEL A question having been asked as to how the Christmas dinner to the inmates of the Workhouse passed off, Mr. JOLLEY said that he had been present and the dinner was a most satisfactory one and seemed to be appreciated most heartily. Everything, as far as he could see, went off remarkably well, and it reflected great credit on the master and matron: The dinner was admirably cooked, , and the plum pudding was Al. He was quite sure that the vote of thanks that was passed to the Board of Guar- dians was very heartfelt and very sincere; it was not Mere Werde.—Mr. QWII.I Wee thm.e any drunkenness, Mr. JOLLEY None whatever.—Mr. GREENING asked why the master had not given them a report; it was the usual thing.—The WORKHOUSE Megrim said he had not given a report because he looked back to last year and saw that he report had been given.—Mr. Darreeserite. said that one of the Guardians asked the question whether there was any drunkenness and Mr. Jolley said there was none. —Mr. JOLLEY : I answered for what I saw .—Mr . DARBYSHIRE: But Mr. Jolley was not there vereleng.—Mr. Joture : I was there an hour.—Mr. DAUBYSHIRE said he was at the workhouse some time after Mr. Jolley and he did not see any drunkenness, but he uaderstood there was drunkenness. Such an appetite was created in some of the inmates by the beer, they had in the house, that there was a steeplechase to get over the walls of the house to procure more drink; it was a sort of butterfly business--ea jumping business. (Laughter). The Matron had done all she could to prevent it, but he was sorry to say she had to write to the Chief Constable to ask him to look after some women belonging to the workhouse, and to get them back again into the workhouse. If such a report as that, was correct, he did not see how Mr. Jolloy could say there was no drunkenness in connection with the Christmas dinner. Although the Christmas dinner was not held on Christmas day to commemorate the birth of our Saviour, it was held on the following day to com- memorate the same object. That was the way the Board of Guardians of Warrington stimulated the inmates to commit such depredations and such disorder as was committed after the beer had had time to work in the inmates and stir them up. (Lauglatar). It could not be expected that the beer would take effect in a minute. ' He was very 'sorry that some of the inmates had misused the confidence that the Guardians had placed in them, but there would not have been that disorder had the in- mates not had beer. It was clear to him that the beer that had been served in the house had created the appe- tite for other beer. It reminded him of the old saying "a pint is refreshment, three gills is ding-dog, and a quart is not half enough." (Laughter.)--Mr. BLACK- HURST : We may make a note ot Chairman said they could not help smiling at the graphic way in which Mr. Derbyshire had described the matter, but at the same time it was distressing to hear it. Before saying anything further he should like to hear what the Workhouse Master had to say about it. (Hear, hear). The WORKHOUSE MASTER said the women referred ' to made their escape . over the wall about three or four o'clock. They had their dinner at 12 o'clock, and they had each a pint of beer, but as some of the inmates might not have drunk a pint others might have had more. They had no more beer between 12 and 3 o'clock, and the men and women had the same quantity of beer. He at first was only going to give them half-a-pint each but Mr. Jolley told him that it was a pint that the Guardians ordered to be given. Four of the women came back within an hour. but they had a difficulty in getting back as the man in the rail- way signal box saw them making desperate attempts to get over. the *all, and they at last paid a man to bring them a ladder. That would be about 5 o'clock. These women were tipsy when they came back to the work- house and one fell down and cut her head.—Mr. Pansy- SHIRK: Have the other two women got back yet P—The WORKHOUSE MASTER said one of them had been sent to gaol for being drunk and disorderly the same day, and the other was on the list as a lunatic.—Mr. JOLLEY' : How many men went out and got drunk ?—The WORKHOUSE MASTER said he had not heard of one and he thought it must have come to his knowledge had there been any.— Mr. JOLLEY : Do you think that a pint of that ale would make either a man or woman drunk P—The Woaxgoess MASTER Said the WOMQII were easily excited. If they had ail-been honest and drunk their own beer only he did not think the pint would make them drunk.—Mr. JOLLEY said that during his stay at the house everything went on in as orderly a manner as any guardian could desire. He had seen no signs of drunkenness or he should not have made the assertion he had done. He could not conceive how a drunken woman or even a drunken man could get over the wall, and he thought there had been some exaggoration in some way. If a person was drunk he' was lielplees.—Mr. DARBYSHILLE said Mr. Jolley had got hold of the wrong end of the tail ; it was not said that the women were drank when they went out; they were then only starting.—Mr. JOLLEY repudiated the remark made about creating a desire for drink. He said it was noth- ing of the sort. There were four or five women who had unsconducted themselves, but the inastAir told them that the men had conducted themselves rightly. But because three or four evil spirits out of 300 or 400 had done this, it should not be said that the whole thing was bad.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said he stayed at the Workhouse a good deal longer than Mr. Jolley, and he and Mr. Ratcliffe stayed at the request of the master to help to keep order. He had voted against the beer being given, and he should after this vote against it with a greater determination. In less than an hour after the beer had been drunk by the inmates the matron had to go down to the women's ward to keep them in order. In the men's side there was nothing but joviality going on, singing and shouting as in a public-house, and ho would say it was more like a public-house at eleven o'clock at night than a workhouse at three o'clock in the afternoon.—Mr. GREENING said he was sorry, but not surprised, at what had taken place. Although not reported in former years, it was his opinion ' that that, sort of thing had always taken place. Various Unions had found that the thing must be put a stop to, and the Salford Guardians were unanimous this year in discontinuing the beer. There were a great many other Unions in the country where beer wa.s not allowed be- , cause of the disordeK it brought about. It was not a ' kindness, but cruelty, to the inmates to give them drink i which brought them to such a disgraceful condition. It was not the fault of the inmates, but that of the Guardians. They were to . blame for the disorder that had taken place in the house, and the sooner they saw an end put to it the better. (Hear, hear.) If the women had not had beer there would not now be one of them ingaol. —Mr. Owee,who remarkedthat theorato7of teetotallers was surprising, contended that all the inmates should not be punished because about half-a-dozen had misbe- haved themselves.—Mr, leurcreeee said he had been at the workhouse at four o'clock in the afternoon of the day that the dinner was given, and at that time there was a little bit of larking amongst the men. He thought half a pint of beer was sufficient, but he did not think all the inmates should be punished because of three or four. They would find even in what they called "civilised life " some people who misbehaved themselves. (Laugh- ter.) He was glad to say that those who had done wrong were Warrington characters, and not "New- toners." (Laughter.)—Mr. W. Houerrrox thought the whole matter had been too highly coloured. He had listened carefully, and he could not see that 'there had been anything very serious. It was Christmas time, and no doubt some little excitement had been induced, but there was'disorder in the house at other times, (especially, among the women.—Mr. DARBY/MIRE I wonder when it would become serious.—The CHAIRMAN said he was very sorry to hear the account that had been related;

WARRINGTON.

The annual treat to this children of the Sunday School connected with, the Working-men's Mission, 'Bank Quay, was held ou Monday evening, and was, as usual, very largely attended.. There sat down between 500 and 600 scholars to an excellent tea, which Was eerved by the teachers of the school. and other friende. 'After tea an entertainment was held, the eAiodlrooin being crowded. The chair was taken by Aldermen J. Crostleld. The choir and scholars, under the conductorship of Mr: Williams, iiikving rendered a song: Mr. .1. itessALL (hon. sec. of.the school) read the annual report, in which he,statecl that dnring the past year thee had had a large increase in the number of'echOlars, Lula they were sorry that they would be unable to admit any More scholars, as the scheolevae now filled to its utmost capacity every Sun- day. The number of scholars on 'the register was— males 279, females 305, total 584, being 114 more than last year. 'The number of teachers was—males 19, fee males 10, three more than last year. The average attend- ance of scholars in the miming was—males 92, females 68, total 160 ; , average attendance in the afternoon— males 182, females 172, total 354, thus making the total average atteedance each day. 504, or an increased attend- anee each day. of 40 over last year. The average attend- antic of teachers in the morrung was—melees 13, females 2; afternoon, males 18, females 5. The finances Of the scheol were in a very satisfactory condition. The trea- surer had a' i balance n hand at the commencement of the year of £2 lie 3d ; the income for the yeer had been £36 13s. 41, making a total of £39 4s. Nel. The expenditure had been £3B is. 9d., leaving a balance of £3 3s. Old. The officers elected for the ensuing year were :—President, Mr. Joseph Monks, senr.; superinten- dents, Mr. David Hill and Mr. James Wooley ; treasurer, .Mr. James 'Wooley ; secretary, 'Mr. John Hassell; visi- tors, Mr. Joseph Monks', seine, and Mr. R. Williamson. The Band of Hope in connection with the school was in a very satisfactory condition, and was, they believed, do- ing a good work, especially amongst the young people. They were pleased to note that Jane Birch, ene of the , members of their Band of Hop*, was succe,sful in obtain- ing one of the 10e. prizes in the competitive examinations open to all the Band a Hopes in the United Kingdom. They. also had a mutual itnnrovement claw, which held very pleasing and instructive Meetings, and they were 51ad to see that the young people Ceutitined to how en i increasing interest n the meetings. A very pleasing feature of the year's work was the formation of a junior class numbering 18 members the majority of whom were scholars of the Sabbath school. Thu unanimity of feeling and the oneness of purpose which had permeated the whole body of teachers throughout the year enabled them to account for the signal success which had attended' their efforts. The. Hon. Secretary also referred to the death of John Harrison in the great storm on the river in the early part of.last year as the dark feature- of the year's history of the miseion.—The Custunsei, in a short address, said he was very glad to be there again that night to meet them at the annual tea party of the chil- dren. The numbers attending teat school had now got so large that they were compelled to make some rule of attendance, and when the teachers mentioned the mattertohim he said that he thought they should not allow any child to go. on Walking Day to Walton Lea or at Christmas time to that tea unless the child had attended at least half the number of times in the year that it was possible to attend. By that means they prevented a child coining perhaps only twice or thrice time in the year and yet being as well treated as a child that had attended perhaps every time. He hoped they wouli see the fairness and propriety of dealing with the matter in that manner. (Hear, hear.) He had been very pleased to hear the excellent report of the secretary. He thought they might safely say that the school was more flourishing now than it had ever been since it com- menced something like 15 years ago. It was wonderful when they remembered that the commencement of that school was in a fustian cutting room on the other side of the road and with about six or eight children, and now their number had swollen until they had got to be up- wards of 500. He was very pleased to see the children with such clean faces and so neatly, dressed, because :it was one half of the education of a Sunday School to have the children neat when they came in. (Hear,hear.) He wanted the parents of the scholars to remember that their indebtedness was very great to the teachers who devoted their Sundays the whole year round to giving them instructions in the Sunday School. It was very good .of the teachers to do it and the children: ought to show their appre- ciation by their regular attendance. (Loud applause.)— Short and suitable addresses were subsequently given by Mr. Monks, Mr. D. Hill, and Mr. T. Dale, and an excel- lent programme of music and song was creditably ren- dered. Amongst those who sang or recited were Miss Ashley, Master J. W. Taylor. Messrs. Mills, Williams, and Haseldine, Mies M. Tilling, Miss E. Tilling, Mies J. Birch, Mister J. Dawber,and Master J. W. Pemberton. A duet on the pianoforte was so cleverly rendered by Master and Miss Crosfield that they received a very hearty recall. A most enjoyable and successful evening was brought' to a dose by the singing of a chorus by the choir.

Sir,—lt has occurred to me that it might be.ot ser- vice if you would kindly insert in your valued and widely circulated papers the followirg few lines as a sort of invitation to your various correspondents. or others. I have often thought it would be interesting to ,many, if someone would write a sort of history of the various industries we have amongst us—the wire manufacturing business, for instance. It would be interesting to know its rise, progress, and present condition. There are other trades—soap, iron, leather, glass, &c. Perhaps someone could give us some interesting facts. If you think such an intimation as this would lead to any good, I should be obliged if you would insert it in your next.—l am, yours truly, WIRE.

[We shall be glad to make room for information of the kind suggested. Those who cannot furnish a history might forward a few notes. Perhaps " Wire " will be good enough to set the example? We hope he will, as he knows something of the trade.—En. Er.l

CALIFORNIA "BOOMING." Sir,—ln a letter recently written by Mrs. Parker there Is a statement respecting the building trade in, Is An. gelos which I think is rather misleading. Mrs. Parker states that 20s. and 245. per day are paid to joiners and builders and that there is great scarcity of workmen. Now, the average rate of wages earned by joiners in the wood factories, where the greatest part of the building -work, is done is 10s. per day, and these are the men who get constant employment. The carpenters who fix up the framing in the blocks or houses, earn about 145., and the bricksetters 20s. per day. The houses are thrown up very quickly, and the men have often to seek fresh jobs which frequently means loss of time. The annexed is a letter publisfied by the . General Union of Carpenters and Joiners. If you will kindly in- sert in your valuable paper you will greatly oblige, yours truly JAMES WLNSTANLEY. • 19, Mill Lane, Warrington, Jan. 4th, 1888. [EXTRACT] Los AsciEtos; Cat., 27th October, 1887. Of the numerous methods adopted to boom the Pacific Coast. there are none so injurious to the workingmen as the exaggerated reports of a scarcity of labour and high wages. Unfortunately the poor dupe who sacrifices his little earthly possessions to enable him to reach these shores in quest of steady work" and "high wages," looks in vain for fulfillment of thesegoldenpromises. Just now Southern California is being extensively advertised as the "promised land" of the poor, ill-paid, slave of labour. In nearly all the paragraphs going the rounds of the press thee is such a misrepresentation of facts, such barefaced falsehoods in regard to wages and the demands for labour, that we have taken upon ourselves to refute them, and thus save hundreds of families from ruin. Already a stream of mechanics and labourers have poured into the city whose ranks are daily beirg. swelled by freqii accessions. Having expended their last dollar for railroad fare, they rush around from one job to another, offering to work for anything they can get. The scenic grandeur fails to impress them, and they find our "glorious climate" rather thin diet to subsist on. We, therefore, ask the Eastern press to aid us in arresting this hegira, and we earnestly entreat them to publish this warning. Periodically, however, aind more often this time of the year, the market has been overcrowded, and only a small number have se- cured the great boon of all workingmen "a home free and unencumbered." The greater number live from band to mouth. Rents are enormously high; a cottage cif four rooms rents from $25.00 to $50.00 a month. Coal is $16.00 a ton, butter 40 cents, eggs 40 cents, and other things in proportion. The average of wages is about fifty cents per day more than Eastern wages, but the cost of living more than counterbalances. Out-of-door labour can be pursued for about ten months in the year; but the man who, attempts it is Sure to break down. Tropical climates will not permit an un- ceasing round of hard manual labour. There is a gra- dual and stealthy undermining process which the vic- tim heeds generally after it is too late to repair the eva. The El Dorado of him who ha l but hlFi two brawny arms to eke out an existence, is not here. We, you fellow workmen, know whereof we speak, therefore, heed our warning. Stay away! Don't come here!

THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC. Sir,-‘-Recurring to Mr. Gladstone's views on the liquor traffic, let me ask you to look at his last statement made a short time ago before the Liberal Federation of Not- tingham. He indicatted there that his political efforts must be centered upon the Irish question, and that noth- ing else could lie done till that was settled. When that ,is settled, he says, and not before, other questions, in- cluding that of the liquor laws, should be taken up, but, he says, he does not expect at his age to take the lead in such matters. When he was in power in 1883 the same disposition seemed prevalent: for then Mr. Hibbert, of the United Kingdom Alliance, asked him about this matter, and received his reply in the year 1885, when he was out of power. Three times, under Mr. Gladstone's ministry, the House of Commons declared for local option legislation, while on the other hand, Home Rule never commanded a majority of the House. Mr. Gladstone ignored the demand for local option, while he bulged out the Home Rule Bill, till, like Pat's big turnip, it grew and pushed all the others out of the field ; and then he cried—" How can I do anything for you when the Home Rule Bill occupies the held'?" But what is the disturbance in Ireland that it should take the place of this great question? Are the, evil results which follow in the train of their bad laws greater that the results of the liquor traffic? I say, no. The I laws of Ireland affect the- people of Ireland alone, and those interestedly connected therewith; but this traffic stretches out the hand of destruction throughout the entire realm. The lawa of Ir land have brought sadness sand poverty to the few of its inhabitants; hut this has Alighted the prospects, ruined the homes, and broken -down the constitutions of millions of our fellow-men, and sent them to their graves without a ray of - We should be far less, surprised if it was that our legislators did not know these facts, but they must be aware of their existence. Has it not been publicly ad- mitted by Mr. Gladstone himself, that the terrible calamities of war, pestilence, and famine are nOt equal in their destructive influences to this mighty evil? Why then have they not endeavoured with more „persistence and greater unanimity to stop it? Is it bePause the people are not really for it? That can be proved to be false. Or are they afraid to entrust into the hands of the people the power to stop it for themselves? Probably nne may fear that we have not sufficient wisdom to vexercise the power if it were given to us. Bilt we have -wisdom, and strength of mind too; for they should re- member that we are men as well as they, and live in the 19th century with them. Or is it that all this untold temporal and eternal misery must exist for the sake of the vested interests of a few big men? It may possibly be that the gold that flows into the revenue ye,w by year is carefully considered and guarded! But by those ceaseless streams of gold, Which into its coffers flow. • . • ;Ought of the mitten's weal lsfold. ' .4 But of the peoples' woe. If a Christian country cannot exist 'efithoutbeing .sup- ported by an infernal prop, it is better that it-ahould not remain, any more thsaa'a dlsristllt;church that cannot live Without the sup Port of blood-money. "Satan does nothing whatever tb .support the Kingdom of Christ." Ah ! sir, it is a pity if our beloved country has to main- tain its present position if glory ,with such blood-stained gold as this; it is a pity if we cannot lawfullji' be rich. Such gold is corrupted, and is built upon human sufferings. But what can ssee. do?, Are teetotal- lars to be the directors of men's minds and actions, and , say--" Do this or that ?" That would be tyranny in the, highest: Undoubtedly there is entrusted to men a free will which ought not to be trampled upon -by others. Time after time we have preached the principles of temperance, but, like the Son of 3.11a.in we have had to lainent as he did over Jerusalem and say "Ye would not." The facts have already been made linown, but the question is—how can we make them more effectual? Our legislators ought to have sufficierit wisdom without our dictation; but, alas! wisdom and righteousness and peacq are all sacrificed to self-interest. I believe it would be far better if we made this a more prominent question , when engaged in the choice of representatives ; for see- ing it endangers ourbrethren, anl even our very selves," it is a matter of great importance, and is worthy of all our concentrated energy. We hope that by-and-by some- thing will be done, directly or indirectly, for its suppres- sion. We shall for the present continue our efforts in training the young, and displaying both by precept and example that temperance is pure and elevating; mean- while faithfully proclaiming with God's ancient prophet —" Woe unto them that call evil good and good evil, that put darkneAs for light and light for darkness, and take the righteousness of the righteous from him."— yours,
JOS. ELLISON.

The tenants on an estate. before adopting the Nan of Campaign, meet, and having fully discussed and care- fully consldered the fall in prices of agricultural produce and failure of crops, decide on the reduction which they will seek from their landlord. These reductions have -aried from 10 to 30 per cent. If their landlord doe.; N t consent to give the required abatement off the rent ft ^ompromise the matter, ete tenants adopt the Plan, ox , lodge their rents (less the abatement) in the hands of and 7.e trustees with the landlord conies to sec the jus- relic?) . their demand. This offer was made by his lordship as he plainly sees that if his tenants go into the Land Court they win gee a still greater reduction, as the undermentioned list of reduc- tions, made by the Sub-Commissioners at Rathkeale, Newcastle West, Bruff, and Thurles amply demonstrate. I might mention that these rack-rents were never paid out of the produce of the land, but were made up by the contributions of the wages of the exiled sons and daughters of these poor tenantry, children who, though thousands of miles of ocean divided them from their native land, have never forgotten it, and who will make any sacrifice to keep their parents in the "old home." _ _ Judicial

Thos. &Donnell 35 0 So far so good. -Here are decisions by a tribunal, which, to put it in the mildest way, is not too fairly dis- posed to the tenants, that for years the landlords have been guilty of the most shameless extortion. The next step, one would think, would be to assess the restitution that should be repaid by the landlords to the tenants. At the very least the arrears of plunder should be abolished. Nothing of the kind. The landlord may evict next day for these arrears. It is not easy to realise the hideous mockery of the system as it stands.- At the very instant that the law declares the rent to be exorbitant, dis- honest, and unbearable, it evicts the tenant, and hands his home and property over to the landlord, because he was not able in the past to pay this exorbitant, dis- honest, and intolerable impossible. The jaw effect a boon with one hand and snatches it away with the other. To the evictor the reductions would be a jest, to the tenant they would be the cruellest mockery if the tenants' organisation was not behind the Courts. I ad- mit the re&ctions are useful as a confession of the jus- tice of tenants' claims, but the Plan of Campaign or the terror of it is needed to give them fort* or vitality. Only a fortnight ago the rent of a holding on Tottenham's es- tate was reduced from £lB to £2. Yet the other week the tenant thereof was evicted and his house levelled to the ground for non-payment of a year's arrears of £lB, of which £2 had been declared by the Land Commission to be the rent, and £lB in excess of a fair rent. Yet the c,oercionists blandly assure us that Irish tenants have nothing on earth to complain Of, and . designate the Plan of Campaign as " pure and simple robbery." I wol leave your readers to decide who are the robbers.—l am, yours truly, RICHARD A. ATKINS, T.C. Cork, Jan., 1388.
FASHIONABLE MARRIA.GE .At HALEWOOD.

On Thu-sday afternoon there was celebrated, in the picturesque little church at Halewood, a mar*. riage between Miss Sybil Harrietta Neilson, youngest daughter of the late Mr. Robert Neilson, Halewood, Deputy-Lieutenant for the County, and Mr William -Lee Pilkington, eldest son of Mr William Pilkington, the present Deputy-Lieutenant of tile County. The ceremony was performed by the Her Thomas Chambers, rector of Halewood. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr){. C. Neilson. and Mr R. Grant Lawson officiated as best man. The bride wore a white brocaded velvet dress, ti:mmed with Brussels lace, and carried a bouquet of Bourbon roses and orange blossoms. The bridesmaids, who were Miss Maude Neilson (eousin of the bride), Misses Ethel and MarPilking- ton '(sisters Of the groom), and Miss Norah Graves, wore dvesses of white broche trimmed withì lace, the bodices trimmed with pearls, and,white velvet hats trimmed with lace and pearls. They each car- ried a bouquet of .Marshal Niel roses. The church was very prettily decorated, for •the occasion, the were pealed, and the organist (Mr. George Lister) played • Mendelssohn's "Wedding March as the party left the church. The ceremony was witnessed by a large and fashionable congregation. who afterwards attended an "At Home" given by Mrs Graves, Woolton, sister of the bride.. The newly-married.couple took train to LOndon,,en route for the South of France and Italy, where the honey- moon is to be spent.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

At the meeting of the Wirral Highway Board, on Monday, the clerk (Mr. W. U. Churton) read a cer- respondence which had taken place between him and the agent of the contractor for the Manchester Ship Canal Works at Eastham and Ellesmere Port, with reference to the damage done to the roads under the jurisdiction of the board by the extraord- inary traffic in connection with the canal works. Durineethe month of November alone the board had expended over and above the amount incurred for the repair and maintenance of the roads in. ordin- ary times the sum of .ElO9 17s Bd, and the clerk, acting under the directions of the board, had for- warded a bill for that amount, accompanied by the surveyor's certificate, to the contractor (Mr. T. A. Walker). The latter, through his agent (Mr. Man- isty), had replied that it, was absurd to send a bill for that amount on the 25th November, seeing that the extra traffic only commenced on the 23th, ,Ocroe ber, and suggested that an accurate account of the cost should be kept for twelve months, and that the- contiactor should only.be called upon to pay the difference between that and the, average for the' last three yetrrs.—Mr. Churton explained that the £lO9 was entirely apart from the ordinary main- tenance and repair, and, was solely the result of the. canal works traffic. He therefore wrote to, 31r: Manisty that he saw no reason why the money should not be paid at once. That gentleman offered' to pay half the sum claimed, but fie (Mr. Churton) could not see how the board multi entertain their. Moreover, during the month of December the board' had incurred farther extraordinary expenditure in connection with the canal work traffic, amounting to-.42l 4s sd.—The clerk was instructed to tab.- proceedings for the recovery of the mondv,i if not' paid paid within a week. There are new upwards of 20fr men. employed upon the Runcorn section of the canal. It is pro- bable that this namber will be greatly increasa4 within the next two months. The work of erectiag huts has commenced at Weston Mint. and Mr. E.: Aaron on Tuesday announced to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority that he had it cregood authority' that 700 men would be labouring in Weston Marsh. in a short time. At Astmoor, near Runcorn, there has arrived a steam navvy, but it is not yet, fixed fbe operations. This wonderful machine is capabheof removing about 1,500 tons per fray, equal to the labour of several Imndred men, and it would seem that the work of excavating is. about to be com- menced in the locality. Messrs. Kirkham and Co are progressing rapidly with the eienstruction of the bridge over the canal at Norte, and the fate of the "Big Field' is being rapidly changed. (Mikes, engine shed, mestroom, storeroom. and hutei for dwellings are beirrgcompleted as fast as i)c.sable. and there will soon be accommodation for many, • hundreds of men. A visit to the course of the Slip Canal at Moore and Acton Grange gives a vivid impression ef the vigoia with whieh,the work of eonstruction is being carried on by the contractor. Over a length of about two miles there are several hundred work- men engagedin the. work of excavating along the centre of the future canal, and' a huge and con- tinuous pile of the soil that has been displaced, which is of a very sandy nature, is being rapidly raised Sllong the whore length. To connect the works with the adjacemi -Runcorn canal a line of rails has been laid down, along which the mate- rial brought on barges aleng the canal is expe- ditiotedv transfim•ed to the scene of operations. Lines of rails have‘also been laid along the cutting, and upon these wagons are run to facilitate the labour of the navvies. Large plies of timber have' been collected, and there is a great abundance of other necessary material. The locality is visited from day to day by large numbers of spectators, who manifest a deep interest in all that is going on. There iá also a constant stream of men in search of work, no so far the supply of labour must have been far ineXcess of the demand. In the other direction the work of canal-making is beingcarried on with equal energy in the neighbourhood of Hollins Green. In this locality the great influx of woek- peekele has turned almost every available dwelling into a lodging-house, and, in additlou, wooden huts are being provided.

THE SAD DROWNING FATALITY AT DITTQN. ' On Tuesday, at the Blackburn e Arms. Ditton, Mr. I Brighouse, the county coroner', resumed the inquiry into the circumstancesattending thedeath of Eliza- beth Taylor, aged 50 years, wife of Frederick Tay- lor, hthourer, 42. Charlotte-street, Widnes. Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor. again watched the proceed- ings for the relatives of the deceased, and Inspector Keighley appeared for. the police.—lt will be re- membered that on Christmam Eve, the deceased, a lod- ger, named John Wilson, and :Mr. and Mrs. Pennington went to Ditton to take part in a raffle "near the New Inn." At this inn they had a Considerable quantity of liquor, and on leaving at clwing time, the lodger and the deceased were very drunk. On the way towards home they fell down several times; and upon being raised the last time, the woman ran away. The man arrived home alone at midnight, and on the 2.80, Dec. the woman's dead body was found in Ditton Brook.— The first witness now called was Dr. McLennan, who had made a posi;-mortem examination of the body. The cause of death, he said, was drowning. The bruise on the breast might have been the result of a fall, but was not sufficient to cause death.—Lowry Miller, landlord of the New Inn, deposed that the four persons got to his house about seven o'clock and left about tenminutes past ten. They were on good terms with each other.—Wll- - Pennington, 45, Charlotte-street, said Mrs Taylor had had a. "sup" before she went to Ditton. On leav- ing the New Inn both Mrs Tailor and her lodger were fresh and they walked arm in arm behind him '(witness) and his wife. The deceased would not be able to walk home without help.—Henry Gasket', of Flgje-road. Ditton, said he was night-foreman at the Liver Alkali Works. About half an hour past midnight on Christmas Eve, he Saw the deceased sitting on the ground in N 0.3 revolver shed. She was drunk, and said she was looking for her husband. This shed was over 100 yards from the entrance to the works. He and Christopher Healey, a fireman, helped her to the gate and saw her into the road. He dare not have kept the woman on the works; it was as much as his placewas woith. He never inquired where the woman lived': she , walked towards Ditton. He could not help her coming' to her death.—The Coroner : You simply found her in the works and turned her out. If she had been allowed to sleep off her drunken fit, her life might have been saved. Witness said she might have wakened up, walked about, and got scalded.. Then the blame would have been upon him— Christopher Healey, labourer, corroborated.—John wheelwright. .40. Lugsdale-rxul. Widnes, depoied' to alighting froth the train at Ditton at 11-35. Near the Liver Works he overtook Sohn Wilsoft, the lodger. Hi did not know the man, who was very drunk and stag- gering about the road. Wilson said. "Will you afire me' y,ur hand? I have had a little drop too much:" He' look the man to Charlotte-street .—P.C. Budsoirdèscribed how he found the body in Ditton Brook, on the. 26th December.—The Coroner said after this evidence it was onl* fair to say that there was no suspicion against . Wilson now, and alluding to the woman being turned out of the works, he remarked that it seemed a rather`harsh ,moceeding. There wat nothing to show that she had come to her death by violence, and he suggested a vev dict of "Found drowned."--After a private consultation the jurrretumed this verdict, and added a rider that they,„were azieed that the woman ought rto have been taker( Mre"hf, 'and net turned out of the world in the sthntrary manner in which she was.
